which serous membrane is attached directly to the outer surface of each lung? visceral pleura parietal pleura visceral pericardium parietal peritoneum visceral layers cover organs (viscera); parietal layers line the cavity walls. "pleura" refers to the lungs, "pericardium" to the heart, and "peritoneum" to the abdominal cavity. so the membrane on the lung surface is the visceral pleura.

which statement uses a directional term incorrectly for a person in anatomical position? the sternum is medial to the arms. the skin is superficial to the skeletal muscles. the nose is anterior to the ears. the knee is proximal to the hip. the hip is closer to the trunk than the knee, so the knee is distal to the hip, not proximal. the sternum is near the midline (medial), the skin is closer to the surface (superficial), and the nose is in front of (anterior to) the ears, so those statements are correct.

homeostasis is best described as keeping every body variable at one exact value at all times the body's repair response that occurs only after an injury keeping internal conditions within a stable range despite outside changes the steady growth of new cells to replace old, worn-out ones homeostasis means keeping internal conditions (temperature, blood glucose, ph) within a narrow normal range. values fluctuate around a set point; they are not frozen at one exact number.

the spinal cord is protected within which body cavity? thoracic cavity vertebral (spinal) cavity pelvic cavity pericardial cavity the dorsal body cavity has two parts: the cranial cavity (brain) and the vertebral cavity (spinal cord). the thoracic, pelvic, and pericardial cavities are all parts of the ventral body cavity.

a patient's chart says a wound is located on the "plantar" surface. where should the nurse look? the sole of the foot the palm of the hand the back of the hand the top of the head plantar refers to the sole of the foot (think "planting" your foot on the ground). the palm is the palmar surface, the back of the hand is dorsal, and the top of the head is the cranial or parietal region.

click the chamber that pumps oxygen-rich blood out to the whole body. oxygen-rich blood (red) comes back from the lungs to the left side of the heart. the left ventricle pumps that blood into the aorta, which carries it to the body. its thick muscular wall gives it the force to do this. the left atrium also holds oxygen-rich blood, but it only passes blood down to the left ventricle. it does not pump blood to the body.

click the valve that blood passes through as it leaves the right atrium. blood in the right atrium flows down into the right ventricle. the valve between them is the tricuspid valve (right atrioventricular valve). it has three flaps. the pulmonary valve is the next valve on the path. blood passes through it when it leaves the right ventricle.

a patient has a narrowed (stenotic) valve. because of it, the left ventricle must work harder to push blood into the aorta. click that valve. blood leaves the left ventricle through the aortic valve and enters the aorta. if the aortic valve is narrowed, the left ventricle must squeeze harder to push blood through the smaller opening. over time its wall thickens. the mitral valve lets blood into the left ventricle, not out of it. the pulmonary valve is on the right side of the heart.

the vessel labeled j carries: oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle to the body oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium oxygen-poor blood from the body to the right atrium j is the pulmonary trunk. it leaves the right ventricle and splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries. it carries oxygen-poor blood (blue) to the lungs to pick up o₂. the aorta (i) carries blood to the body, the pulmonary veins (m) bring blood back from the lungs, and the venae cavae (k, l) bring blood back from the body.

when the left ventricle contracts, which lettered valve closes so that blood does not flow back into the left atrium? e g f h the valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle is the mitral (bicuspid) valve, f. when the ventricle contracts, the rising pressure snaps the mitral valve shut, so blood can only leave through the aortic valve (h). e is the tricuspid valve (right side), and g is the pulmonary valve.

a red blood cell has just left the superior vena cava. put these structures in the order it passes through them, first to last. right atrium tricuspid valve right ventricle pulmonary valve pulmonary trunk the superior vena cava empties oxygen-poor blood into the right atrium. from the right atrium, blood passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. the right ventricle pumps it through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk, which carries it toward the lungs.

using the diagram, which vessels carry oxygen-rich blood? select all that apply. aorta pulmonary veins pulmonary trunk superior vena cava inferior vena cava the pulmonary veins bring freshly oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. the aorta carries that same oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle to the body. the pulmonary trunk carries oxygen-poor blood to the lungs. the superior and inferior venae cavae return oxygen-poor blood from the body. the common trap is thinking all veins carry oxygen-poor blood. the pulmonary veins are the exception in adults.

put these structures in the order that oxygen-poor blood passes through them on its way from the body to the lungs. superior and inferior venae cavae right atrium tricuspid valve right ventricle pulmonary valve oxygen-poor blood from the body returns through the venae cavae into the right atrium. it passes the tricuspid (right av) valve into the right ventricle. the right ventricle pumps it through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and arteries toward the lungs.

put these structures in the order that oxygen-rich blood passes through them, starting from the lungs. pulmonary veins left atrium mitral (bicuspid) valve left ventricle aorta oxygen-rich blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. it flows through the mitral (bicuspid) valve into the left ventricle. the left ventricle pumps it through the aortic valve into the aorta and out to the body.

which vessel carries oxygen-poor blood from the heart to the lungs? pulmonary vein aorta pulmonary artery superior vena cava arteries carry blood away from the heart, even when that blood is low in oxygen. the pulmonary arteries take oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs; the pulmonary veins bring oxygen-rich blood back.

which chamber of the heart has the thickest muscular wall? right ventricle left ventricle left atrium right atrium the left ventricle pumps blood through the entire systemic circulation, which has much higher resistance than the lungs. it needs the most muscle (myocardium) to generate that pressure. the right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs, and the atria just push blood into the ventricles.

which structure is the heart's natural pacemaker? sinoatrial (sa) node atrioventricular (av) node purkinje fibers bundle of his the sa node in the wall of the right atrium fires on its own fastest, so it sets the heart rate. the av node, bundle of his, and purkinje fibers conduct the signal it starts.

put the parts of the cardiac conduction system in the order the electrical impulse travels through them. sa node av node bundle of his (av bundle) right and left bundle branches purkinje fibers the impulse starts at the sa node and spreads across the atria, which contract. the av node briefly delays it so the ventricles can fill. it then travels down the bundle of his, the bundle branches, and the purkinje fibers, which make the ventricles contract from the apex upward.

which valve is located between the left atrium and the left ventricle? tricuspid valve aortic valve pulmonary valve mitral (bicuspid) valve the left atrioventricular valve has two cusps, so it is called the bicuspid or mitral valve. the tricuspid valve is on the right side; the aortic and pulmonary valves are semilunar valves at the exits of the ventricles.

exchange of oxygen, nutrients, and wastes between the blood and body tissues takes place across the walls of which vessels? arteries veins capillaries arterioles capillary walls are a single layer of endothelial cells, thin enough for substances to diffuse through. arteries, arterioles, and veins have thicker walls and mainly serve to carry blood.

which of the following are formed elements (cells or cell fragments) of the blood? select all that apply. erythrocytes (red blood cells) leukocytes (white blood cells) platelets albumin water formed elements are the cells and cell fragments: red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets (fragments of megakaryocytes). albumin (a plasma protein) and water are parts of plasma, the liquid portion of blood.

a patient with a very low platelet count is at greatest risk for which problem? frequent bacterial infections excessive bleeding and bruising low blood oxygen levels dangerously high blood pressure platelets (thrombocytes) form a plug at an injury and help start clotting. too few platelets means bleeding is hard to stop. frequent infections suggest low white blood cells; low oxygen suggests too few red blood cells (anemia).

a patient has left-sided heart failure, meaning the left ventricle cannot pump blood forward effectively. fluid will most likely back up into which organs first? lungs liver and abdomen ankles and feet kidneys blood returning from the lungs enters the left side of the heart. if the left ventricle fails, blood backs up into the pulmonary veins and lungs, causing pulmonary congestion and shortness of breath. swelling of the ankles, feet, and liver is typical of right-sided failure, because blood backs up into the systemic veins.

a patient's blood pressure is 128/82 mm hg. what does the 128 represent? pressure in the arteries when the ventricles relax (diastolic) the number of times the heart beats per minute the pressure inside the right atrium of the heart pressure in the arteries when the ventricles contract (systolic) the top number is systolic pressure: the peak arterial pressure during ventricular contraction (systole). the bottom number (82) is diastolic pressure, during ventricular relaxation. heart rate is measured separately in beats per minute.

why do many veins in the legs contain valves? to raise blood pressure in the veins above arterial pressure to allow gas exchange with surrounding tissues to prevent blood from flowing backward away from the heart to pump blood the way the heart does blood pressure in veins is low, and blood in the legs must return to the heart against gravity. one-way valves keep blood moving toward the heart while skeletal muscles squeeze the veins. valves do not pump on their own; the surrounding muscle contractions provide the push.

a blockage in a coronary artery most directly deprives which tissue of oxygen? the lung tissue (alveoli) the myocardium (heart muscle) the brain (cerebral cortex) the inner lining of the aorta the coronary arteries branch off the aorta and supply the heart muscle itself. a blocked coronary artery causes a myocardial infarction (heart attack), in which heart muscle cells die from lack of oxygen.

a patient's heart rate is 75 beats per minute and the stroke volume is 70 ml per beat. what is the cardiac output in liters per minute? (cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume.) cardiac output = 75 beats/min × 70 ml/beat = 5,250 ml/min. convert to liters: 5,250 ml ÷ 1,000 = 5.25 l/min. a normal resting adult cardiac output is about 5 l/min, so this answer is reasonable.

which blood type is considered the universal donor for red blood cells? o negative ab positive a negative b positive type o negative red blood cells have no a, b, or rh (d) antigens on their surface. with no antigens to react to, they can be given to nearly any recipient in an emergency. ab positive is the universal recipient, the opposite idea.

a patient has type a blood. which antibodies are normally present in this patient's plasma? anti-a antibodies only both anti-a and anti-b antibodies no abo antibodies anti-b antibodies only type a red blood cells carry a antigens. the plasma contains antibodies against the antigen the person does not have, so type a blood has anti-b antibodies. if this patient received type b blood, the anti-b antibodies would attack the donor cells.

which statements about arteries are correct? select all that apply. they carry blood away from the heart. they have thicker muscular walls than veins. they always carry oxygen-rich blood. they contain one-way valves along their length. they carry blood at higher pressure than veins. arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure, so they have thick, muscular, elastic walls. not all arteries carry oxygen-rich blood: the pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs. valves along the vessel are a feature of veins, not arteries.

what is the name of the double-layered sac that surrounds the heart? pleura peritoneum pericardium myocardium the pericardium encloses the heart; fluid between its layers reduces friction as the heart beats. the pleura surrounds the lungs, the peritoneum lines the abdominal cavity, and the myocardium is the heart muscle itself.

the first heart sound ("lub") is caused by which event? closing of the aortic and pulmonary (semilunar) valves closing of the tricuspid and mitral (av) valves contraction of the atria opening of the av valves when the ventricles begin to contract, pressure rises and snaps the av valves shut, producing "lub." "dub" is the second sound, when the semilunar valves close as the ventricles relax. valve opening is normally silent.

in adults, where are red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets produced? red bone marrow spleen liver lymph nodes hematopoiesis (blood cell formation) in adults takes place in red bone marrow, found in bones such as the hip bones, sternum, and vertebrae. the spleen removes old red blood cells, the liver makes plasma proteins, and lymph nodes house lymphocytes but do not make all blood cells.

the hepatic portal vein carries nutrient-rich blood from the stomach and intestines directly to which organ? heart kidneys spleen liver after a meal, absorbed nutrients travel in the hepatic portal vein to the liver before reaching the rest of the body. this lets the liver process nutrients, store glucose as glycogen, and detoxify drugs and toxins first.

click the trachea (windpipe). the trachea is the tube that runs from the larynx down into the chest, where it splits into the two primary bronchi. c-shaped rings of cartilage (the stripes in the drawing) hold it open. the esophagus lies behind the trachea and carries food, not air.

click the flap of cartilage that covers the opening of the larynx during swallowing, so food goes into the esophagus instead. the epiglottis is a leaf-shaped flap of elastic cartilage at the top of the larynx. when you swallow, the larynx rises and the epiglottis folds down over its opening. food and drink slide back into the esophagus. if this fails, food or liquid can be aspirated into the airway. nurses watch for this in patients with swallowing problems (dysphagia).

click the tiny air sac where gas exchange with the blood takes place. gas exchange happens in the alveoli. these are tiny, thin-walled air sacs at the ends of the bronchioles. each alveolus is wrapped in capillaries. o₂ diffuses from the alveolus into the blood, and co₂ diffuses from the blood into the alveolus. the capillary is a blood vessel, not an air sac.

which lettered structure contains the vocal cords? d b c e the vocal cords (vocal folds) are inside the larynx, or voice box, labeled d. b is the pharynx (throat), which carries both food and air. c is the epiglottis, which covers the larynx during swallowing. e is the trachea, below the larynx.

air has just entered the nasal cavity. put these structures in the order the air passes through them on the way to the alveoli. pharynx larynx trachea primary bronchus bronchioles from the nasal cavity, air moves back into the pharynx (throat), then down through the larynx (voice box). next comes the trachea, which branches into the right and left primary bronchi. the bronchi keep branching into smaller and smaller bronchioles, which end at the alveoli.

in the close-up, blood flows through capillary i from left to right. compared with the blood entering at the left, the blood leaving at the right has: less o₂ and more co₂ more o₂ and more co₂ about the same o₂ and co₂ more o₂ and less co₂ gases diffuse from high concentration to low concentration. air in the alveolus has more o₂ than the blood arriving from the body, so o₂ moves into the blood. the blood has more co₂ than the alveolar air, so co₂ moves out of the blood. the blood leaves with more o₂ and less co₂. that is why the capillary is drawn changing from blue to red.

in pulmonary edema, fluid builds up in and around the alveoli. why does this lower the patient's blood oxygen level? the fluid thickens the barrier between alveolus and capillary, so o₂ diffuses more slowly. the fluid collects in the trachea and blocks air from reaching the lungs. the fluid makes the diaphragm contract harder, pushing air out of the alveoli. the fluid reacts with o₂ in the alveoli and changes it into co₂. o₂ reaches the blood by diffusing across the very thin wall between the alveolus and the capillary. diffusion is fastest when that barrier is thin. fluid makes the distance t

put these structures in the order inhaled air passes through them, starting at the nose. nasal cavity pharynx larynx trachea primary bronchi air enters the nasal cavity, where it is warmed, moistened, and filtered. it passes through the pharynx (throat) and larynx (voice box) into the trachea. the trachea splits into the right and left primary bronchi, one to each lung.

put these airways in order from largest to smallest as air moves deeper into the lung. trachea primary bronchus secondary (lobar) bronchus bronchiole alveolus the trachea branches into primary bronchi, which branch into secondary (lobar) bronchi, one per lobe. bronchi keep branching into tiny bronchioles, which end in clusters of alveoli where gas exchange occurs.

which muscle does most of the work during quiet breathing? pectoralis major rectus abdominis trapezius diaphragm the diaphragm is the primary muscle of inspiration; the external intercostals help. abdominal muscles assist only with forced exhalation, and the pectoralis major and trapezius move the arm and shoulder.

gas exchange between the lungs and the blood takes place in tiny air sacs called ______. the alveoli are thin-walled sacs surrounded by capillaries. oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood, and carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli.

which change occurs during normal inspiration (inhalation)? the diaphragm relaxes and domes upward, decreasing the volume of the thoracic cavity air pressure inside the lungs rises above the atmospheric pressure outside the diaphragm contracts and flattens, increasing the volume of the thoracic cavity the external intercostal muscles relax, and the ribs move downward and inward when the diaphragm contracts it moves downward, and the external intercostals lift the ribs, so the chest cavity gets bigger. bigger volume means lower pressure in the lungs (boyle's law), so air flows in from the highe

which structure folds over the opening of the larynx during swallowing to keep food out of the airway? uvula epiglottis vocal cords pharyngeal tonsil the epiglottis is a flap of elastic cartilage that covers the laryngeal opening (glottis) when you swallow. the uvula and soft palate close off the nasal cavity, not the larynx.

a baby born at 28 weeks of gestation struggles to keep the alveoli from collapsing after each breath. a deficiency of which substance is most likely the cause? surfactant hemoglobin mucus cilia surfactant is made by type ii alveolar cells and lowers surface tension inside the alveoli. without enough surfactant, alveoli collapse at the end of each exhalation, making breathing exhausting. the lungs do not make enough surfactant until late in pregnancy, so premature infants are at risk.

oxygen moves from the alveoli into the pulmonary capillary blood by which process? active transport by atp-powered membrane pumps osmosis through the respiratory membrane filtration driven by capillary blood pressure diffusion down its partial pressure gradient alveolar air has a higher partial pressure of oxygen than the blood arriving at the lungs. oxygen therefore diffuses down its gradient across the thin respiratory membrane; no atp is needed. osmosis refers to the movement of water, not gases.

in a healthy person, which change is the strongest chemical stimulus to increase the rate and depth of breathing? a small drop in blood oxygen level a rise in blood glucose level a rise in blood carbon dioxide level a drop in core body temperature chemoreceptors in the medulla and in the carotid and aortic bodies are most sensitive to co₂ and the h⁺ (lower ph) it forms. even a small rise in co₂ quickly increases ventilation. oxygen must fall quite low before it becomes the main drive in a healthy person.

which part of the brain contains the main centers that set the basic rhythm of breathing? cerebellum medulla oblongata occipital lobe thalamus respiratory centers in the brainstem, especially the medulla oblongata (with help from the pons), set the breathing rhythm. the cerebellum coordinates movement, the occipital lobe processes vision, and the thalamus relays sensory information.

how is most of the carbon dioxide carried in the blood from the tissues to the lungs? as bicarbonate ions (hco₃⁻) in plasma bound to the iron atoms in hemoglobin as dissolved carbon dioxide gas in plasma attached to the surface of platelets about 70% of co₂ reacts with water inside red blood cells (sped up by carbonic anhydrase) to form carbonic acid, which becomes h⁺ and hco₃⁻. the bicarbonate moves into the plasma and is carried to the lungs. smaller amounts travel bound to hemoglobin's protein part (not the iron, where o₂ binds) or dissolved as gas.

which structure is known as the "voice box" because it contains the vocal cords? pharynx trachea bronchus larynx the larynx sits on top of the trachea and contains the vocal folds, which vibrate to produce sound. the pharynx is the throat; the trachea is the windpipe.

the right lung has three lobes, but the left lung has only two. what is the best explanation? the liver sits directly beneath the left lung and compresses it the left primary bronchus is wider and shorter than the right one the heart takes up space on the left side of the thoracic cavity the left lung does not take part in gas exchange with the blood the heart tilts toward the left, so the left lung is smaller and has an indentation called the cardiac notch. the liver lies under the right side of the diaphragm, and both lungs exchange gases. in fact, the right primary bronchus is the wider, mo

smoking damages the ciliated cells that line the trachea and bronchi. which function is most directly impaired? exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide across the alveolar walls sweeping mucus and trapped particles out of the airways producing surfactant to keep the alveoli open contracting the diaphragm during each inhalation the airways are lined with cells whose cilia beat to push mucus (and trapped dust and microbes) up toward the pharynx, where it is swallowed or coughed out. when cilia are damaged, mucus builds up, causing "smoker's cough" and more infections.

during an asthma attack, which change is the main reason air flow is reduced? bronchiole smooth muscle contracts, narrowing the airways the alveoli fill with blood and stop exchanging gases the diaphragm becomes paralyzed and cannot contract the cartilage rings of the trachea soften and collapse asthma involves inflammation and spasm of the smooth muscle in bronchiole walls (bronchoconstriction), plus extra mucus. narrower airways increase resistance, causing wheezing and difficulty exhaling. rescue inhalers work by relaxing this smooth muscle (bronchodilation).

a longtime smoker from merced is diagnosed with emphysema, in which the walls between alveoli are destroyed. why does this reduce oxygen uptake? the airways become lined with extra cilia that block airflow the blood loses its ability to carry carbon dioxide the alveoli make so much surfactant that they stick shut less surface area is available for gas exchange breaking down the walls between alveoli merges many small sacs into fewer large ones. fewer, larger sacs have much less total surface area, so less oxygen can diffuse into the blood. the lungs also lose elastic recoil, so air gets trappe

which structure is a shared passageway for both food and air? larynx trachea pharynx esophagus the pharynx (throat) carries air to the larynx and food to the esophagus. the larynx and trachea carry only air, and the esophagus carries only food.

tidal volume is best defined as the maximum amount of air that can be exhaled after a deep breath the volume of air moved in or out in one normal, quiet breath the air that remains in the lungs after a forced exhalation the number of breaths a person takes per minute at rest tidal volume is the normal resting breath, about 500 ml in an adult. the maximum exhaled after a maximum inhale is vital capacity, the air left over is residual volume, and breaths per minute is respiratory rate.

which are functions of the nasal cavity? select all that apply. warming incoming air moistening (humidifying) incoming air trapping dust and microbes in mucus exchanging oxygen with the blood producing surfactant the nasal cavity's mucous membrane and rich blood supply warm and moisten air, and hairs and mucus filter it. gas exchange happens only in the alveoli, and surfactant is made by alveolar cells.

a student having a panic attack breathes very rapidly and deeply (hyperventilates). what happens to the blood? co₂ decreases and ph rises (more basic) co₂ increases and ph falls (more acidic) co₂ decreases and ph falls (more acidic) co₂ increases and ph rises (more basic) hyperventilation exhales co₂ faster than the body makes it, so blood co₂ falls. less co₂ means less carbonic acid and fewer h⁺ ions, so ph rises: respiratory alkalosis. this can cause dizziness and tingling in the fingers and lips.

what is the main function of the pleural fluid between the two pleural membranes? exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide with the blood producing antibodies against inhaled microbes moving mucus toward the pharynx reducing friction as the lungs expand and recoil the visceral and parietal pleurae are separated by a thin film of serous fluid. the fluid lets the lungs glide smoothly against the chest wall and also helps the membranes cling together so the lungs follow the chest wall as it expands.

which events occur during normal, quiet exhalation? select all that apply. the diaphragm relaxes and moves upward the volume of the thoracic cavity decreases air pressure in the lungs rises slightly above atmospheric pressure the external intercostal muscles contract the abdominal muscles contract forcefully quiet exhalation is passive: the diaphragm and external intercostals relax, and the elastic lungs recoil. thoracic volume shrinks, so lung pressure rises above atmospheric pressure and air flows out. contracting the external intercostals is part of inhalation, and forceful abdominal contra

click the organ where most chemical digestion and nutrient absorption take place. the small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum) is where most chemical digestion is finished and most nutrients are absorbed. enzymes from the pancreas and bile from the liver and gallbladder are added in the duodenum, and folds, villi, and microvilli give it a huge surface for absorption. the stomach starts protein digestion, but it absorbs very little. the large intestine mainly absorbs water and electrolytes.

click the organ that stores and concentrates bile. the gallbladder is the small sac tucked under the liver. it stores bile and concentrates it until a fatty meal arrives. then it contracts and squeezes bile into the duodenum, where the bile emulsifies fats. trap: the liver makes bile, but the gallbladder stores it.

click the muscular tube that carries swallowed food from the throat to the stomach. the esophagus connects the pharynx (throat) to the stomach. waves of muscle contraction called peristalsis push food along it. that is why you can swallow even lying down. no digestion or absorption happens in the esophagus. it only moves food.

organ f releases digestive enzymes into the small intestine and releases insulin into the blood. what is organ f? gallbladder liver pancreas stomach f is the pancreas, which lies behind and below the stomach, with its head inside the curve of the duodenum. it is both an exocrine gland (enzymes and bicarbonate sent through a duct to the duodenum) and an endocrine gland (insulin and glucagon released into the blood). the gallbladder (d) stores bile, the liver (c) makes bile, and the stomach (e) makes acid and pepsin. none of these makes insulin.

a patient is diagnosed with hepatitis, which is inflammation of the liver. which letter marks the affected organ? d c e f "hepat-" means liver, and "-itis" means inflammation. the liver is c, the large organ in the upper right of the abdomen (on the viewer's left in a front view). d is the gallbladder, e is the stomach, and f is the pancreas.

accessory digestive organs help digestion by making or storing substances, but food never passes through them. which lettered organs are accessory organs? select all that apply. c d e f g c (liver) makes bile, d (gallbladder) stores bile, and f (pancreas) makes digestive enzymes. ducts carry these to the duodenum, but food never travels through these organs. e (stomach) and g (small intestine) are parts of the gi tract (alimentary canal). food passes right through them. other accessory structures are the teeth, tongue, and salivary glands.

put these parts of the gi tract in the order that food passes through them, first to last. esophagus stomach small intestine large intestine rectum after swallowing, food goes down the esophagus to the stomach. from the stomach it moves into the small intestine (duodenum first), then into the large intestine (colon). waste is stored in the rectum before it leaves through the anus.

put these organs in the order food passes through them, from first to last. mouth esophagus stomach small intestine large intestine food is chewed in the mouth, swallowed through the pharynx and esophagus, and churned in the stomach. most digestion and absorption finish in the small intestine, and the large intestine absorbs water and forms feces.

put these regions of the intestines in the order that food residue passes through them. duodenum jejunum ileum cecum ascending colon the small intestine runs duodenum → jejunum → ileum ("dow jones industrial"). the ileum empties through the ileocecal valve into the cecum, the first part of the large intestine. from the cecum, material moves up the ascending colon, then across the transverse colon and down the descending colon.

in which organ does most absorption of nutrients take place? small intestine stomach large intestine esophagus the small intestine is long and has a huge surface area, so it absorbs most nutrients. the stomach absorbs only a few substances (such as alcohol), and the large intestine mainly absorbs water and electrolytes.

what is the main purpose of the villi and microvilli that line the small intestine? to produce bile for fat digestion to push food along the tract by peristalsis to store food in the intestine until it is digested to increase the surface area for absorption villi are finger-like folds, and microvilli are tiny projections on each absorptive cell (the "brush border"). together they multiply the surface area, so more nutrients can be absorbed. peristalsis is done by smooth muscle layers, and bile is made by the liver.

which statement about bile is correct? it is produced by the gallbladder and stored in the liver it is produced by the pancreas and stored in the gallbladder it is produced by the liver and stored in the gallbladder it is produced by the stomach and stored in the duodenum liver cells (hepatocytes) make bile continuously. the gallbladder stores and concentrates bile, then releases it into the duodenum when fatty food arrives.

what is the main role of bile in digestion? breaking down proteins into amino acids emulsifying fats into smaller droplets digesting starch into glucose neutralizing the stomach's acid in the stomach itself bile salts break large fat globules into tiny droplets (emulsification), the way dish soap breaks up grease. this gives lipase much more surface area to work on. bile has no digestive enzymes of its own.

chemical digestion of starch (carbohydrate) begins in which location? the mouth, by salivary amylase the stomach, by pepsin the small intestine, by lipase the large intestine, by bacteria salivary glands release amylase, which starts breaking starch into smaller sugars while you chew. pepsin digests protein, and lipase digests fat. pancreatic amylase continues starch digestion in the small intestine.

chemical digestion of protein begins in which organ? mouth large intestine esophagus stomach chief cells in the stomach release pepsinogen, which hydrochloric acid converts into the active enzyme pepsin. pepsin begins breaking proteins into smaller peptides; pancreatic enzymes finish the job in the small intestine.

which enzyme breaks down dietary fats (triglycerides)? amylase pepsin lipase lactase "lip-" refers to lipids (fats), so lipase digests fats into fatty acids and monoglycerides. amylase digests starch, pepsin digests protein, and lactase digests the milk sugar lactose.

peristalsis is best described as the chemical breakdown of food by digestive enzymes wavelike smooth muscle contractions that move food along the absorption of nutrients through the intestinal wall chewing and grinding food into smaller pieces rings of smooth muscle contract behind a food mass and relax ahead of it, squeezing it forward. peristalsis moves food down the esophagus and through the stomach and intestines; it does not chemically digest food.

what is the main function of the large intestine? absorbing water and electrolytes and forming feces producing bile and most digestive enzymes absorbing most of the nutrients from digested food beginning the chemical digestion of protein by the time material reaches the large intestine, most nutrients have already been absorbed. the large intestine reabsorbs much of the remaining water and electrolytes, compacting the residue into feces. this is why problems that speed material through the colon cause watery diarrhea.

a patient had her gallbladder removed (cholecystectomy). which type of meal is she most likely to have trouble digesting comfortably? a meal high in starch a meal high in lean protein a meal high in fiber a large, high-fat meal the gallbladder stores concentrated bile and releases a large amount when fatty food enters the duodenum. without it, bile trickles in continuously from the liver, so there may not be enough at once to emulsify a large fatty meal. starch and protein digestion depend mainly on enzymes, not bile.

bacteria living in the large intestine produce a vitamin needed to make blood clotting factors. a patient on long-term antibiotics may become deficient in which vitamin? vitamin c vitamin a vitamin k vitamin d normal gut bacteria in the colon synthesize vitamin k, which the liver uses to make several clotting factors. long antibiotic courses can kill these bacteria, lowering vitamin k and increasing bleeding risk. vitamin d is made in the skin with sunlight, not by gut bacteria.

a patient has frequent heartburn because stomach acid flows back into the esophagus (gerd). weakness of which structure is most likely responsible? pyloric sphincter lower esophageal (cardiac) sphincter ileocecal valve internal anal sphincter the lower esophageal sphincter at the stomach's entrance normally keeps acidic stomach contents out of the esophagus. the pyloric sphincter is at the stomach's exit, and the ileocecal valve and anal sphincter are much farther down the tract.

which structure controls the passage of chyme from the stomach into the duodenum? pyloric sphincter lower esophageal sphincter ileocecal valve epiglottis the pyloric sphincter is a ring of smooth muscle at the bottom (pylorus) of the stomach. it releases small amounts of chyme at a time so the duodenum is not overwhelmed.

which is a function of the hydrochloric acid (hcl) secreted in the stomach? it emulsifies dietary fats into droplets so lipase can digest them it absorbs water from food it digests starch into maltose it activates pepsin and kills many swallowed microbes hcl makes the stomach very acidic (ph about 2). this acid converts inactive pepsinogen into pepsin and destroys many bacteria in food. bile emulsifies fat, and amylase digests starch.

which of the following are functions of the liver? select all that apply. producing bile detoxifying drugs and alcohol storing glucose as glycogen secreting insulin absorbing most nutrients from digested food the liver makes bile, breaks down drugs, alcohol, and toxins, and stores glucose as glycogen (it also makes plasma proteins like albumin). insulin is secreted by beta cells of the pancreas, and most nutrient absorption occurs in the small intestine.

the semi-liquid mixture of partly digested food and gastric juice that leaves the stomach is called ______. the stomach churns food with gastric juice into a soupy mixture called chyme. chyme passes through the pyloric sphincter into the duodenum. (do not confuse it with chyle, the fatty lymph in lacteals.)

pancreatic juice contains bicarbonate (hco₃⁻). what is its main role? emulsifying fats into small droplets activating pepsin so it can digest proteins in the stomach neutralizing acidic chyme as it enters the duodenum killing bacteria in the large intestine chyme leaving the stomach is very acidic. bicarbonate from the pancreas neutralizes it, protecting the intestinal lining and providing the near-neutral ph that pancreatic enzymes need.

which of the following are accessory digestive organs, meaning food does not pass through them? select all that apply. liver pancreas gallbladder stomach esophagus accessory organs help digestion by making or storing secretions (bile, enzymes) that flow into the gi tract through ducts. the stomach and esophagus are part of the alimentary canal (gi tract) itself, so food passes through them.

a patient's skin and the whites of the eyes appear yellow (jaundice) because of a buildup of bilirubin. which organ is most likely involved? stomach liver large intestine small intestine bilirubin comes from the breakdown of old red blood cells and is normally processed by the liver and excreted in bile. liver disease (such as hepatitis or cirrhosis) or a blocked bile duct lets bilirubin build up in the blood, turning tissues yellow.

carbohydrates must be digested into which form before they can be absorbed by the small intestine? monosaccharides, such as glucose amino acids fatty acids and glycerol disaccharides, such as sucrose only single sugars (monosaccharides like glucose, fructose, and galactose) can be absorbed. brush-border enzymes such as sucrase and lactase split disaccharides into monosaccharides first. amino acids come from protein, and fatty acids come from fat.

which letter marks the part of the neuron that receives signals from other neurons? g d e a dendrites (a) are the short, branched extensions that receive incoming signals and carry them toward the cell body. d is the axon, which carries the impulse away from the cell body. g marks the axon terminals, which send the signal on to the next cell. e is the myelin sheath.

in the synapse close-up, click the gap where neurotransmitter molecules diffuse from one neuron to the next. when an impulse reaches the axon terminal, synaptic vesicles release neurotransmitter by exocytosis. the neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft, the narrow gap between the two cells, and binds to receptors on the receiving neuron. the vesicles store the neurotransmitter. the cleft is the space it crosses.

in multiple sclerosis (ms), the immune system damages structure e. what is the most direct effect on the neuron? the cell body can no longer make proteins. synaptic vesicles can no longer store neurotransmitter. dendrites can no longer receive any signals. impulses travel more slowly along the axon, or fail to get through. e is the myelin sheath, the fatty insulation wrapped around the axon. myelin lets the impulse jump from node to node (saltatory conduction), which makes it fast. when myelin is damaged, conduction slows or is blocked. this causes ms symptoms such as weakness, numbness, and v

click the part of the brain that coordinates balance and smooth, precise movements. the cerebellum ("little brain") sits below the occipital lobe at the back of the head. it compares planned movements with what the body is actually doing, keeping movements smooth and balanced. damage to it causes ataxia: a wide, unsteady gait and clumsy movements. that is why a field sobriety test checks balance, since alcohol impairs the cerebellum.

after a brain injury, a patient's heart rate, blood pressure, and basic breathing rhythm become unstable. click the region that contains the control centers for these vital functions. the medulla oblongata is the lowest part of the brainstem, just above the spinal cord. it contains the cardiac, vasomotor (blood pressure), and respiratory rhythm centers, so injury here can be life-threatening. the pons, just above it, helps adjust breathing. but the centers for heart rate and blood pressure are in the medulla. the cerebellum controls coordination, not vital functions.

which lettered lobe processes visual information from the eyes? a c b d vision is processed in the occipital lobe, c, at the back of the cerebrum. a (frontal) handles planning, decisions, and voluntary movement. b (parietal) handles touch and body position. d (temporal) handles hearing and memory. a hard hit to the back of the head can cause "seeing stars" or vision loss because it injures the occipital lobe.

click the layer of the eye that contains the photoreceptors (rods and cones). the retina is the inner layer lining the back of the eye. its rods (dim light) and cones (color) change light into nerve signals. these signals leave the eye through the optic nerve. the sclera is the tough white outer layer, and the choroid (the dark layer between them) is full of blood vessels. neither one detects light.

put these structures in the order light passes through them on its way to the photoreceptors, first to last. cornea pupil lens vitreous humor retina light first passes through the clear cornea, which does most of the bending (refraction). it goes through the pupil, the opening in the iris, and then through the lens, which fine-tunes the focus. it crosses the gel-like vitreous humor and lands on the retina, where rods and cones detect it.

which lettered structure changes shape to focus light from near or far objects onto the retina? a b f d d is the lens. tiny ciliary muscles pull on it or relax so it becomes flatter or rounder. this is called accommodation. a (cornea) bends light even more than the lens does, but its shape is fixed. b (iris) changes the size of the pupil to control how much light enters. f (retina) detects the light.

what is the basic functional cell of the nervous system that transmits electrical signals? nephron neuron neuroglia (glial cell) osteocyte neurons generate and conduct electrical impulses. glial cells support and protect neurons, a nephron is the kidney's functional unit, and an osteocyte is a bone cell.

put these parts in the order a signal travels through a neuron, from where it is received to where it is passed on to the next cell. dendrites cell body axon axon terminals dendrites receive incoming signals and pass them to the cell body. the impulse travels down the axon to the axon terminals, which release neurotransmitter onto the next cell.

a nurse taps a patient's patellar tendon and the leg kicks. put the parts of this reflex arc in order. sensory receptor in the muscle sensory (afferent) neuron integration center in the spinal cord motor (efferent) neuron effector (quadriceps muscle) a stretch receptor detects the stimulus and a sensory neuron carries the signal to the spinal cord. the signal is processed in the spinal cord (for the knee-jerk, the sensory neuron synapses directly on the motor neuron). a motor neuron carries the command to the effector, the quadriceps, which contracts.

what is the main function of the myelin sheath that wraps many axons? it increases the speed of nerve impulse conduction it produces neurotransmitters for the synapse it receives incoming signals from other neurons it stores calcium ions needed for muscle contraction myelin is a fatty insulating layer formed by schwann cells (pns) and oligodendrocytes (cns). impulses jump from one gap in the myelin (node of ranvier) to the next, which is much faster than in unmyelinated axons. in multiple sclerosis, loss of cns myelin slows or blocks signals.

a patient with damage to the cerebellum would most likely have trouble with which function? understanding and producing spoken language regulating body temperature seeing colors and recognizing faces balance and coordination of movement the cerebellum compares intended movements with actual movements and fine-tunes them, so damage causes clumsy, unsteady movements. language is handled mainly in the cerebral cortex, temperature by the hypothalamus, and vision by the occipital lobe.

during a summer heat wave in fresno, which brain region detects the rising body temperature and triggers sweating? cerebellum occipital lobe hypothalamus medulla oblongata the hypothalamus is the body's thermostat; it also regulates hunger, thirst, and the pituitary gland. when blood temperature rises, it signals sweat glands to secrete and skin blood vessels to dilate.

a stroke damaging the occipital lobe of the cerebrum would most likely affect which function? hearing vision smell balance the occipital lobe at the back of the brain contains the primary visual cortex. hearing is processed in the temporal lobe, and balance relies on the cerebellum and inner ear.

which response is caused by the sympathetic ("fight-or-flight") division of the autonomic nervous system? pupils dilate and heart rate increases digestion speeds up and salivation increases pupils constrict and heart rate slows the bladder contracts to empty sympathetic activation prepares the body for emergencies: faster heart rate, dilated pupils and bronchioles, and more glucose released into the blood. digestion, salivation, pupil constriction, and bladder emptying are "rest-and-digest" parasympathetic responses.

which of the following are effects of the parasympathetic nervous system? select all that apply. slowing the heart rate stimulating digestion constricting the pupils dilating the bronchioles releasing glucose from the liver the parasympathetic division ("rest and digest") slows the heart, increases digestive activity, and constricts the pupils. dilating the bronchioles and raising blood glucose are sympathetic (fight-or-flight) effects.

which of the following are part of the peripheral nervous system (pns)? select all that apply. cranial nerves spinal nerves ganglia (clusters of neuron cell bodies outside the cns) spinal cord cerebellum the cns is the brain (including the cerebellum) and the spinal cord. everything outside them, including cranial nerves, spinal nerves, and ganglia, belongs to the pns.

during depolarization of a neuron's membrane in an action potential, which ion movement occurs? potassium ions (k⁺) rush into the cell chloride ions (cl⁻) rush out of the cell calcium ions (ca²⁺) are pumped out of the cell sodium ions (na⁺) rush into the cell when voltage-gated na⁺ channels open, na⁺ flows into the cell, making the inside more positive (depolarization). repolarization follows when k⁺ channels open and k⁺ flows out of the cell. the na⁺/k⁺ pump later restores the resting ion distribution.

which neurotransmitter is released by motor neurons at the neuromuscular junction to stimulate skeletal muscle? dopamine serotonin acetylcholine insulin motor neurons release acetylcholine (ach), which binds receptors on the muscle fiber and triggers an action potential. dopamine and serotonin act mainly in the brain, and insulin is a hormone, not a neurotransmitter.

which layer of the eye contains the light-sensitive photoreceptor cells? cornea retina iris sclera the retina at the back of the eye contains rods and cones that convert light into nerve signals. the cornea bends incoming light, the iris controls pupil size, and the sclera is the tough white outer coat.

which photoreceptors are responsible for color vision and sharp detail in bright light? cones rods hair cells ganglion cells cones work best in bright light and come in types sensitive to different wavelengths, allowing color vision. rods are more sensitive in dim light but see only shades of gray. hair cells are receptors in the inner ear.

put these structures in the order that sound vibrations travel through them on the way to the brain. external auditory canal tympanic membrane (eardrum) ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) cochlea cochlear branch of the vestibulocochlear nerve sound waves travel down the ear canal and vibrate the eardrum. the three ossicles of the middle ear amplify the vibration and pass it to the oval window. fluid waves in the cochlea bend hair cells, which trigger signals in the cochlear nerve to the brain.

a patient reports severe dizziness and a spinning sensation when turning her head. which inner-ear structures detect rotation of the head? cochlea ossicles eustachian (auditory) tube semicircular canals the three semicircular canals are filled with fluid that moves when the head rotates, bending hair cells that signal the brain. the cochlea is for hearing, the ossicles transmit sound, and the eustachian tube equalizes middle-ear pressure.

which structure of the eye changes shape to focus light on the retina for near or distant objects? iris pupil lens optic nerve ciliary muscles adjust the curvature of the lens (accommodation) to focus images on the retina. the iris and pupil control how much light enters, and the optic nerve carries signals to the brain.

which colored, muscular part of the eye controls the size of the pupil? retina iris cornea lens the iris contains smooth muscle that constricts or dilates the pupil to control how much light enters. the pupil is the opening; the iris is the colored ring around it.

the narrow region between the axon terminal of one neuron and the next cell, across which neurotransmitters diffuse, is called the synaptic ______. a synapse is the junction between a neuron and another cell. the narrow space within the synapse is the synaptic cleft; neurotransmitter diffuses across it and binds receptors on the next cell.

a patient has a stroke that damages the motor cortex in the left cerebral hemisphere. where would muscle weakness most likely appear? on the right side of the body on the left side of the body on both sides of the body equally only in the muscles of the eyes most motor pathways cross to the opposite side (decussate) in the brainstem. so the left hemisphere controls voluntary movement on the right side of the body, and vice versa.

what is a main function of cerebrospinal fluid (csf)? carrying oxygen to the bones of the skull producing myelin for axons transmitting nerve impulses between neurons at synapses cushioning and protecting the brain and spinal cord csf fills the ventricles of the brain and the space around the brain and spinal cord. it acts as a shock absorber, makes the brain buoyant, and carries nutrients and wastes. a lumbar puncture (spinal tap) collects csf to test for infections such as meningitis.

which neurons carry information from sensory receptors toward the central nervous system? motor (efferent) neurons interneurons sensory (afferent) neurons schwann cells afferent neurons "arrive" at the cns with sensory information. efferent (motor) neurons "exit" the cns to muscles and glands, and interneurons connect neurons within the cns. schwann cells are glial cells, not neurons.

tap the longest and strongest bone in the body, the bone of the thigh. the femur runs from the hip joint to the knee. it is the longest, heaviest and strongest bone in the body. the tibia and fibula are in the lower leg, below the knee. the humerus is the long bone of the upper arm.

which bone is labeled h? ulna humerus radius fibula h points to the forearm bone on the thumb side (lateral side, with palms facing forward). that bone is the radius. the ulna (g) is the other forearm bone, on the little-finger side. the humerus (e) is in the upper arm, and the fibula (m) is in the lower leg.

a patient at a fresno clinic fell on an outstretched hand and has a fracture of the forearm bone on the thumb side, just above the wrist. tap the bone that is broken. in anatomical position (palms forward), the thumb side of the forearm is the lateral side. the lateral forearm bone is the radius. a fall on an outstretched hand very often breaks the distal radius, near the wrist. the ulna is the medial (little-finger side) forearm bone, so it is the trap answer.

the axial skeleton forms the central axis of the body. which of the labeled bones belong to the axial skeleton? select all that apply. skull sternum ribs clavicle pelvic girdle (hip bones) the axial skeleton is the skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum (plus small bones like the hyoid). the clavicle is part of the pectoral (shoulder) girdle, and the hip bones form the pelvic girdle. girdles attach the limbs, so they belong to the appendicular skeleton.

in an adult long bone, red bone marrow that makes blood cells is found mainly in the region labeled: h d c g g points to spongy bone in the epiphysis. the spaces between its thin plates of bone hold red marrow, which makes blood cells. h is the medullary cavity of the diaphysis. in adults it is filled mostly with yellow marrow (fat). d is dense compact bone, and c is the periosteum, the membrane that covers the outside of the bone.

what is the job of the articular cartilage shown at the ends of the bone? it makes red blood cells for the body it gives a smooth, slippery surface that reduces friction in the joint it anchors tendons and ligaments to the shaft of the bone it stores fat as an energy reserve articular cartilage is a thin layer of hyaline cartilage covering the ends of bones where they meet in a joint. its smooth surface lets bones glide past each other with little friction and helps absorb shock. red marrow makes blood cells, the periosteum anchors tendons and ligaments, and yellow marrow stores fat.

a 10-year-old's x-ray shows a band of cartilage in the place where this adult bone has the epiphyseal line. what happens at that band of cartilage in the child? blood cells are made and released into the blood the bone grows in diameter by adding layers under the periosteum the bone grows in length calcium is removed from the bone to raise blood calcium in children, the epiphyseal (growth) plate is a layer of hyaline cartilage between the epiphysis and diaphysis. new cartilage forms and is replaced by bone, so the bone gets longer. when growth stops after puberty, the plate turns to bone and l

compare the relaxed and contracted sarcomeres. which region stays the same length when the muscle contracts? h zone i band sarcomere (z line to z line) a band the a band is the full length of the thick (myosin) filaments. filaments do not shorten, so the a band stays the same length. thin (actin) filaments slide toward the m line, which pulls the z lines closer together. the sarcomere, the i band and the h zone all get shorter. in the diagram, the myosin rows are the same length in both sarcomeres, but the z lines are much closer together when contracted.

tap a thick filament, the protein whose heads grab and pull the thin filaments during contraction. thick filaments are made of myosin. myosin heads bind actin, pivot (the power stroke) and pull the thin filaments toward the center of the sarcomere. this pulling uses atp and requires calcium to expose binding sites on actin. the thin filaments attached to the z lines are actin.

how many bones are in the typical adult human skeleton? 106 270 206 312 the adult skeleton has 206 bones. newborns have about 270 bony parts, but many fuse together (for example, in the skull and sacrum) during growth.

which type of muscle tissue is striated and involuntary? skeletal muscle cardiac muscle smooth muscle both skeletal and smooth muscle cardiac muscle has striations (stripes) like skeletal muscle but is controlled involuntarily. skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary; smooth muscle is non-striated and involuntary.

smooth muscle is found mainly in which location? the walls of hollow organs, such as the stomach attached to bones of the skeleton by tendons only in the walls of the heart chambers in the tongue and the muscles of facial expression smooth muscle lines hollow organs: the gi tract, blood vessels, bladder, uterus, and airways. skeletal muscle attaches to bones (and forms the tongue and facial muscles), and cardiac muscle is found only in the heart.

a soccer player at fresno state twists her ankle and is told she has a sprain. which structure is injured? a tendon a bone skeletal muscle fibers a ligament a sprain is a stretched or torn ligament; ligaments connect bone to bone at a joint. a strain is an injury to a muscle or tendon (tendons connect muscle to bone), and a fracture is a broken bone.

put these events of skeletal muscle contraction in order, from first to last. a motor neuron releases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction an action potential spreads along the muscle fiber membrane calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum myosin heads bind to actin, forming cross-bridges thin filaments slide toward the center of the sarcomere acetylcholine binds receptors on the muscle fiber, starting an action potential that travels along the membrane and into the t-tubules. this signals the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release ca²⁺, which binds troponin and moves tropom

during skeletal muscle contraction, calcium ions bind to which protein, allowing myosin to reach the binding sites on actin? myosin collagen troponin hemoglobin at rest, tropomyosin covers the myosin-binding sites on actin. calcium binds troponin, which shifts tropomyosin out of the way so cross-bridges can form.

after death, muscles become stiff (rigor mortis). what is the best explanation? without calcium, actin and myosin cannot bind without atp, myosin heads cannot detach from actin acetylcholine is released continuously after death the bones lose calcium and lock the joints in place myosin needs a fresh molecule of atp to release from actin after each power stroke. after death, atp production stops, so cross-bridges stay locked and muscles stiffen. calcium actually leaks into the cytoplasm after death, which allows binding; it does not prevent it.

the thick filaments in a sarcomere are made mainly of which protein? myosin actin keratin collagen thick filaments are myosin, whose heads form cross-bridges. thin filaments are mainly actin (with troponin and tropomyosin). keratin is in skin and hair, and collagen is in connective tissues.

which bone cells break down bone tissue, releasing calcium into the blood? osteoblasts osteocytes chondrocytes osteoclasts osteoclasts dissolve (resorb) bone matrix. osteoblasts build new bone, osteocytes are mature bone cells that maintain the matrix, and chondrocytes are cartilage cells.

which of the following are characteristics of skeletal muscle tissue? select all that apply. striated (striped) appearance under voluntary control long cells with many nuclei found in the walls of blood vessels cells joined by intercalated discs skeletal muscle fibers are long, multinucleated, striated cells that we control voluntarily. smooth muscle lines blood vessel walls, and intercalated discs join cardiac muscle cells.

which bone is part of the axial skeleton? femur scapula sternum clavicle the axial skeleton forms the body's central axis: skull, vertebral column, ribs, and sternum. the femur (limb), scapula, and clavicle (pectoral girdle) belong to the appendicular skeleton.

which type of joint allows the widest range of motion, including rotation in many directions? hinge joint, such as the elbow ball-and-socket joint, such as the shoulder pivot joint, such as between the first two vertebrae suture, such as between skull bones in a ball-and-socket joint, the rounded head of one bone fits into a cup of another, allowing movement in all planes. hinge joints move in one plane, pivot joints allow rotation around one axis, and sutures are essentially immovable.

the sutures that join the bones of an adult skull are classified as fibrous, immovable joints synovial, freely movable joints cartilaginous, slightly movable joints ball-and-socket joints sutures are fibrous joints in which bones are bound by dense connective tissue and essentially do not move (synarthroses). synovial joints have a fluid-filled cavity and move freely; cartilaginous joints like the intervertebral discs move slightly.

an older woman is diagnosed with osteoporosis after a hip fracture. which imbalance best describes what has been happening in her bones? bone building by osteoblasts has exceeded bone breakdown by osteoclasts cartilage has gradually replaced compact bone red bone marrow has replaced all of the yellow marrow bone breakdown by osteoclasts has exceeded bone building by osteoblasts bone is constantly remodeled; in osteoporosis, resorption outpaces formation, so bones lose mass and become porous and fragile. after menopause, falling estrogen allows osteoclast activity to increase, which is why olde

bending the elbow so the hand moves toward the shoulder is an example of which movement? extension abduction flexion rotation flexion decreases the angle between two bones at a joint. straightening the elbow is extension, abduction moves a limb away from the midline, and rotation turns a bone around its own axis.

raising your arm out to the side, away from the midline of the body, is called adduction abduction flexion supination abduction moves a body part away from the midline (think "abducted" = taken away). adduction brings it back toward the midline (you "add" it back to the body). supination turns the palm to face up or forward.

which vitamin is needed for the intestine to absorb calcium, supporting healthy bones? vitamin d vitamin c vitamin b12 vitamin a active vitamin d (calcitriol) increases calcium absorption from the small intestine. without enough vitamin d, bones become soft (rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults). vitamin c is needed for collagen, but it does not control calcium absorption.

which of the following are functions of the skeletal system? select all that apply. supporting the body and protecting internal organs storing calcium and phosphate producing blood cells in red bone marrow producing most of the body's heat secreting digestive enzymes bones support and protect (the skull protects the brain, the ribs protect the heart and lungs), store minerals, and house red marrow that makes blood cells. most body heat comes from contracting skeletal muscle, and digestive enzymes come from digestive glands.

bone-forming cells that secrete new bone matrix are called ______. osteoblasts build bone by laying down collagen and helping it mineralize. once surrounded by matrix, an osteoblast becomes an osteocyte.

when the biceps brachii contracts to flex the elbow, the triceps brachii relaxes. in this movement, the triceps is acting as the prime mover (agonist) synergist fixator antagonist the prime mover (here the biceps) is mainly responsible for the movement. the antagonist (the triceps) opposes that movement and must relax for it to happen; it is the prime mover for elbow extension.

the diaphragm is made of which type of muscle tissue? smooth muscle cardiac muscle skeletal muscle dense connective tissue only the diaphragm is a skeletal muscle controlled by the phrenic nerves. breathing usually happens automatically, but you can also control it voluntarily (holding your breath), which fits skeletal muscle.

osteoarthritis, common in older adults, mainly involves the wearing away of which tissue? red bone marrow articular cartilage covering the ends of bones the periosteum covering the shaft of the bone the tendons and skeletal muscles that cross the joint in synovial joints, smooth hyaline (articular) cartilage covers the bone ends and reduces friction. in osteoarthritis this cartilage breaks down, so bone rubs on bone, causing pain and stiffness.

which labeled organ filters blood and removes old, worn-out red blood cells? a b c d c is the spleen, in the upper left part of the abdomen (on your right as you face the figure). the spleen filters blood, removes old red blood cells and holds lymphocytes that respond to blood-borne germs. a is the tonsils, b is the thymus, and d is the thoracic duct.

tap the organ where t lymphocytes (t cells) mature. it is large in children and shrinks after puberty. the thymus sits in the upper chest, behind the sternum and above the heart. immature t cells travel from red bone marrow to the thymus, where they mature and learn not to attack the body's own cells. after puberty the thymus slowly shrinks and is replaced by fat.

a patient has an infected cut on the hand. a day later, tender, swollen lumps appear in the armpit. tap the type of structure that is swollen. lymph from the hand and arm drains to the axillary (armpit) lymph nodes. lymph nodes filter lymph. when they trap germs, lymphocytes inside multiply, so the nodes swell and become tender. the spleen filters blood, not lymph, and it is in the abdomen, not the armpit.

what is structure d, and where does it return lymph to the blood? thoracic duct; into the left subclavian vein thoracic duct; directly into the right atrium right lymphatic duct; into the right subclavian vein inferior vena cava; into the right atrium d is the thoracic duct. it starts in the abdomen and runs up through the chest just left of the midline. it drains lymph from about three-fourths of the body and empties into the left subclavian vein near the base of the neck. the right lymphatic duct is much shorter and drains only the upper right part of the body.

put the steps in the path of lymph in order, from first to last. fluid between cells enters lymphatic capillaries lymph flows through lymphatic vessels lymph is filtered in lymph nodes lymph collects in the thoracic duct lymph enters the blood at the left subclavian vein extra tissue fluid enters tiny, blind-ended lymphatic capillaries and is now called lymph. lymph travels through larger lymphatic vessels that pass through lymph nodes, where it is filtered. vessels join into large ducts. the thoracic duct returns lymph to the blood at the left subclavian vein.

which of the following are functions of the lymphatic system? select all that apply. returning excess tissue fluid to the blood absorbing dietary fats from the small intestine carrying oxygen to the tissues housing lymphocytes that fight infection producing bile to digest fats the lymphatic system returns leaked tissue fluid to the blood, which helps prevent swelling (edema). lacteals (lymphatic capillaries in the small intestine) absorb dietary fats. lymph nodes, the spleen, the thymus and the tonsils house lymphocytes. red blood cells carry oxygen, and the liver makes bile.

which labeled structure is a patch of lymphatic tissue in the throat that traps germs entering through the mouth and nose? a b e c a points to the tonsils, at the back of the throat (pharynx). tonsils trap inhaled and swallowed pathogens and start an immune response. b is the thymus, c is the spleen, and e points to lymph nodes.

which of the following is part of the body's first line of defense against pathogens? antibodies made by plasma cells cytotoxic t cells that kill infected cells fever that slows pathogen growth intact skin and mucous membranes the first line of defense consists of physical and chemical barriers that keep pathogens out: skin, mucous membranes, tears, stomach acid. fever and inflammation are part of the second (internal innate) line, and antibodies and t cells are the adaptive third line.

which of the following are part of innate (nonspecific) immunity? select all that apply. inflammation fever phagocytosis by neutrophils antibody production by plasma cells memory t cells innate defenses respond quickly and the same way to many different invaders: inflammation, fever, and phagocytes such as neutrophils. antibodies from plasma cells and memory t cells are adaptive: they target specific antigens and remember them.

which cells produce and secrete antibodies? helper t cells neutrophils plasma cells red blood cells when a b cell is activated by its specific antigen, it multiplies and many of its offspring become plasma cells. plasma cells are antibody factories; helper t cells help activate b cells but do not make antibodies.

hiv damages the immune system mainly by destroying which cells? red blood cells (erythrocytes) helper t cells (cd4⁺ cells) platelets plasma cells (from b cells) hiv infects and destroys cd4⁺ helper t cells. helper t cells coordinate both antibody and cell-mediated responses, so losing them weakens the whole adaptive immune system and leads to opportunistic infections.

which cells directly kill body cells that are infected with a virus? cytotoxic t cells helper t cells b lymphocytes (b cells) basophils cytotoxic (cd8⁺) t cells recognize viral antigens displayed on infected cells and release chemicals that kill those cells. helper t cells coordinate the response, b cells make antibodies (via plasma cells), and basophils release histamine.

which white blood cells are the most abundant in blood and usually the first to arrive at a site of bacterial infection? lymphocytes eosinophils monocytes neutrophils neutrophils make up about 50–70% of white blood cells and quickly leave the blood to phagocytize bacteria. a high neutrophil count often signals a bacterial infection. pus is largely made of dead neutrophils.

which of the following are classic signs of inflammation at an injured site? select all that apply. redness swelling heat paleness (pallor) pain inflammation dilates local blood vessels (redness and heat) and makes them leakier (swelling). swelling and chemicals released by damaged cells cause pain. the area becomes red, not pale, because more blood flows to it.

a nursing student receives the hepatitis b vaccine before starting clinicals. which type of immunity does this produce? passive, artificially acquired active, naturally acquired active, artificially acquired passive, naturally acquired a vaccine exposes the body to antigens, so the student's own immune system makes antibodies and memory cells: active immunity. because it comes from a medical intervention instead of a natural infection, it is artificially acquired.

a newborn receives antibodies from the mother through breast milk. which type of immunity is this? active, naturally acquired passive, naturally acquired passive, artificially acquired active, artificially acquired the infant receives ready-made antibodies rather than making its own, so the immunity is passive (and temporary, with no memory cells). it happens through a normal process (nursing or transfer across the placenta), so it is naturally acquired.

a child who had chickenpox is exposed to the virus again years later and does not get sick. what best explains this? memory b and t cells mount a faster, stronger secondary response the virus can no longer infect skin cells neutrophils permanently surround the virus the first infection destroyed all the body's receptors for the virus during the first infection, some activated lymphocytes became long-lived memory cells. on re-exposure, memory cells respond quickly and produce large amounts of antibody, usually before symptoms develop. this immunological memory is the basis for how vaccines work

during a throat infection, the lymph nodes in the neck become swollen and tender. why? the nodes are producing extra red blood cells bile is backing up into the lymph vessels the nodes are storing excess dietary fat lymphocytes in the nodes are multiplying lymph nodes filter lymph and are packed with lymphocytes and macrophages. when they encounter antigens from the infection, lymphocytes multiply rapidly, enlarging the nodes.

besides immune defense, what is a major function of the lymphatic system? pumping blood from the heart to the lungs producing digestive enzymes for the intestine returning excess tissue fluid to the blood filtering urea out of the blood into urine some fluid leaks out of capillaries and is not reabsorbed; lymphatic vessels collect this fluid (lymph) and return it to veins near the heart. if lymph vessels are blocked or removed (for example, after some cancer surgeries), fluid builds up and causes swelling (lymphedema). lymphatic vessels in the intestine (lacteals) also absorb dietary fats.

put the steps of phagocytosis by a macrophage in order. the phagocyte recognizes and attaches to the microbe the phagocyte engulfs the microbe, enclosing it in a phagosome a lysosome fuses with the phagosome lysosomal enzymes digest the microbe the phagocyte first binds the microbe (antibodies or complement coating it make this easier). it wraps its membrane around the microbe, forming a vesicle called a phagosome. a lysosome fuses with it, and digestive enzymes destroy the microbe.

in which organ do t lymphocytes mature? thyroid gland thymus spleen tonsils t cells form in red bone marrow, then travel to the thymus (t for thymus) to mature. the thymus is largest in childhood and shrinks with age. the thyroid is an endocrine gland, not a lymphatic organ.

which organ filters blood, removes old and damaged red blood cells, and is located in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen? spleen liver thymus appendix the spleen filters blood, breaks down worn-out red blood cells, and contains lymphocytes that respond to blood-borne pathogens. the liver is mainly in the right upper quadrant, and the thymus is in the chest.

the y-shaped proteins made by plasma cells that bind to specific antigens are called ______. antibodies (immunoglobulins) bind specific antigens. binding can neutralize toxins, clump microbes together, and mark them for destruction by phagocytes.

an antigen is best defined as a y-shaped protein made by plasma cells a type of white blood cell that engulfs and digests bacteria a chemical released by the brain to cause fever a molecule that triggers a specific immune response antigens are usually proteins or large carbohydrates (on microbes, pollen, or transplanted cells) that trigger an immune response. antibodies are the proteins made to bind antigens; do not mix up the two.

during an allergic reaction to almond pollen, mast cells release a chemical that dilates blood vessels and causes itching and a runny nose. which chemical is this? insulin hemoglobin histamine acetylcholine mast cells (and basophils) release histamine, which dilates blood vessels and makes them leaky. this causes redness, swelling, itching, and mucus, which is why antihistamines relieve allergy symptoms.

a patient develops sudden airway swelling, wheezing, and a dangerous drop in blood pressure minutes after a bee sting (anaphylaxis). which medication is given first to reverse these effects? insulin epinephrine an antibiotic a blood thinner anaphylaxis is a whole-body allergic reaction with massive histamine release. epinephrine constricts blood vessels (raising blood pressure) and relaxes bronchiole smooth muscle (opening airways), which is why it is given right away by auto-injector. antibiotics treat bacterial infections and do nothing for an allergic reaction.

which lymphatic tissues, located in the walls of the pharynx, trap pathogens that are inhaled or swallowed? tonsils lymph nodes of the groin thymus spleen the tonsils are clusters of lymphatic tissue around the throat that sample and fight microbes entering through the mouth and nose. inflamed tonsils (tonsillitis) are a common sign of a throat infection. the thymus is in the chest, the spleen is in the abdomen, and the inguinal lymph nodes are in the groin.

which of the following is an autoimmune disease, in which the immune system attacks the body's own tissues? influenza strep throat valley fever (coccidioidomycosis) type 1 diabetes mellitus in type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys the insulin-producing beta cells of the pancreas. influenza (virus), strep throat (bacterium), and valley fever (a fungus common in central valley soil) are infections caused by outside pathogens.

macrophages, the large phagocytes found in tissues, develop from which type of white blood cell? neutrophils lymphocytes monocytes basophils monocytes circulate in the blood, then leave it and enlarge into macrophages in the tissues. macrophages engulf microbes and debris and present antigens to t cells, linking innate and adaptive immunity.

tap the gland that releases insulin and glucagon to control blood glucose. the pancreas lies behind the stomach, with its head on the body's right and its tail toward the body's left. its islet cells release insulin (lowers blood glucose) and glucagon (raises blood glucose). the adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys and release cortisol and epinephrine.

tap the gland often called the "master gland." it controls several other glands but is itself controlled by the hypothalamus. the pituitary gland hangs from the base of the brain on a thin stalk, just below the hypothalamus. it releases hormones such as tsh, acth, fsh, lh and growth hormone that control other glands. the hypothalamus sends releasing hormones (and nerve signals) to the pituitary, so it is the pituitary's boss.

a patient's blood calcium level is low. tap the glands that release the hormone that raises blood calcium. (use the back view of the neck.) low blood calcium triggers the parathyroid glands to release parathyroid hormone (pth). pth raises blood calcium by releasing calcium from bone, reducing calcium loss in the urine and activating vitamin d so the gut absorbs more. the thyroid makes calcitonin, which lowers blood calcium, so tapping the thyroid is the trap answer. the parathyroids are the small glands on the back of the thyroid.

which gland is labeled f, and which hormone does it produce? adrenal gland; cortisol pancreas; insulin adrenal gland; thyroxine kidney; aldosterone f points to the small glands that sit on top of the kidneys. these are the adrenal glands. the adrenal cortex makes cortisol and aldosterone, and the adrenal medulla makes epinephrine. thyroxine comes from the thyroid. the kidney (h) does not make aldosterone, although aldosterone acts on the kidney.
