which labeled gland secretes melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep–wake cycle? a b d c c is the pineal gland, a small gland deep in the brain. the pineal gland releases melatonin mostly at night, in darkness, which helps set the sleep–wake (circadian) rhythm. a is the hypothalamus, b is the pituitary, and d is the thyroid.

a patient feels tired and cold. lab results show a high tsh level and a low t4 (thyroxine) level. which labeled gland is most likely underactive? pituitary thyroid hypothalamus parathyroid glands tsh from the pituitary tells the thyroid to make t4. normally, high t4 shuts tsh off (negative feedback). low t4 with high tsh means the pituitary is shouting at the thyroid, but the thyroid is not answering. the thyroid is underactive (primary hypothyroidism). if the pituitary were the problem, tsh would be low, not high. the parathyroids control calcium, not t4.

which of the labeled glands are located inside the skull? select all that apply. hypothalamus thyroid pineal pituitary adrenal glands the hypothalamus and pineal gland are part of the brain, and the pituitary hangs from the base of the brain in a pocket of bone in the skull. the thyroid is in the front of the neck, and the adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys in the abdomen.

insulin is produced by which cells? beta cells of the pancreatic islets alpha cells of the pancreatic islets cells of the adrenal cortex liver cells (hepatocytes) the pancreatic islets (islets of langerhans) contain beta cells, which secrete insulin, and alpha cells, which secrete glucagon. the liver responds to insulin, but it does not make it.

name the hormone that lowers blood glucose by helping glucose enter body cells. after a meal, rising blood glucose stimulates pancreatic beta cells to release insulin. insulin helps glucose enter muscle and fat cells and signals the liver to store glucose as glycogen.

between meals, blood glucose begins to drop. which hormone is released to raise it, and how does it work? insulin; it signals the liver to store glucose glucagon; it signals muscle cells to absorb more glucose calcitonin; it releases glucose from bone glucagon; it signals the liver to break down glycogen into glucose pancreatic alpha cells release glucagon when blood glucose falls. glucagon tells the liver to break down stored glycogen and release glucose into the blood. insulin has the opposite effect, lowering blood glucose.

a patient with type 2 diabetes has high blood glucose even though the pancreas is still producing insulin. what is the most likely explanation? the immune system has destroyed all of the beta cells the liver has completely stopped making glucagon body cells have become resistant to insulin's effects the kidneys are secreting too much insulin into the blood in type 2 diabetes, cells respond poorly to insulin (insulin resistance), so glucose stays in the blood. destruction of beta cells by the immune system describes type 1 diabetes. the kidneys do not produce insulin.

which structure releases hormones that directly control secretion by the anterior pituitary gland? thyroid gland hypothalamus adrenal cortex pineal gland the hypothalamus releases releasing and inhibiting hormones that travel through a portal system to the anterior pituitary. because it controls the pituitary, the hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems.

a farmworker in fresno county is becoming dehydrated during a 108 °f afternoon. which hormone increases to help the kidneys conserve water? antidiuretic hormone (adh) insulin calcitonin melatonin when blood becomes more concentrated, the hypothalamus signals the posterior pituitary to release adh. adh makes the kidney's collecting ducts reabsorb more water, producing a smaller volume of concentrated urine. (aldosterone also helps by retaining sodium, but it was not offered as a choice.)

a patient with hyperthyroidism (too much thyroid hormone) would most likely show which set of signs? weight gain, slow heart rate, and cold intolerance low blood calcium, muscle cramps, and spasms very high blood glucose and frequent urination only weight loss, rapid heart rate, and heat intolerance thyroid hormones (t₃ and t₄) raise the body's metabolic rate. too much speeds everything up: weight loss despite eating, fast heart rate, nervousness, and feeling hot. weight gain, a slow heart rate, and feeling cold describe hypothyroidism.

which mineral must be supplied in the diet for the thyroid gland to make its hormones t₃ and t₄? iron calcium iodine potassium t₃ and t₄ contain iodine atoms (the numbers refer to how many each has). a lack of dietary iodine can cause an enlarged thyroid (goiter); iodized salt prevents this.

blood calcium is too low. which hormone is released, and from which gland, to raise it? calcitonin, from the thyroid gland in the neck parathyroid hormone, from the parathyroids insulin, from the pancreas aldosterone, from the adrenal cortex parathyroid hormone (pth) raises blood calcium by stimulating osteoclasts, increasing calcium reabsorption by the kidneys, and activating vitamin d. calcitonin from the thyroid has the opposite effect and lowers blood calcium.

blood levels of thyroid hormone (t₃ and t₄) rise above normal. through negative feedback, what happens next? trh and tsh secretion decrease trh and tsh secretion increase the thyroid gland releases even more t₃ and t₄ the adrenal medulla releases more tsh high t₃ and t₄ inhibit the hypothalamus (trh) and anterior pituitary (tsh). less tsh means less stimulation of the thyroid, so hormone levels fall back toward normal. tsh comes from the anterior pituitary, not the adrenal medulla.

put these steps of thyroid hormone regulation in order. the hypothalamus releases thyrotropin-releasing hormone (trh) the anterior pituitary releases thyroid-stimulating hormone (tsh) the thyroid gland releases t₃ and t₄ body cells increase their metabolic rate trh from the hypothalamus stimulates the anterior pituitary to release tsh. tsh travels in the blood to the thyroid, which releases t₃ and t₄. these hormones raise cellular metabolism, and high levels feed back to slow trh and tsh release.

which gland secretes epinephrine (adrenaline) during a sudden fight-or-flight emergency? adrenal cortex posterior pituitary thyroid gland adrenal medulla the adrenal medulla, the inner part of each adrenal gland, is stimulated by sympathetic nerves to release epinephrine and norepinephrine. the adrenal cortex (outer part) makes steroid hormones such as cortisol and aldosterone.

aldosterone, from the adrenal cortex, causes the kidneys to excrete more sodium and more water into the urine reabsorb more glucose reabsorb sodium (and water) and excrete potassium produce more red blood cells aldosterone acts on the distal tubules and collecting ducts to reabsorb na⁺ and secrete k⁺. water follows sodium by osmosis, so blood volume and blood pressure increase.

which hormone is released by the adrenal cortex during long-term stress and raises blood glucose while suppressing inflammation? epinephrine cortisol oxytocin calcitonin cortisol, a glucocorticoid, raises blood glucose by promoting glucose formation and breakdown of stored fuels. it also suppresses inflammation and the immune response, which is why cortisol-like drugs (such as prednisone) are used for inflammatory conditions. epinephrine is the short-term stress hormone from the adrenal medulla.

which gland secretes melatonin, a hormone that helps regulate the sleep–wake cycle? pineal gland pituitary gland thymus thyroid gland the pineal gland, deep in the brain, releases melatonin mainly in darkness, helping make you sleepy at night.

which hormones are produced and secreted by the anterior pituitary gland? select all that apply. growth hormone (gh) thyroid-stimulating hormone (tsh) prolactin oxytocin insulin the anterior pituitary makes gh, tsh, prolactin, acth, fsh, and lh. oxytocin (and adh) are made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. insulin comes from beta cells of the pancreas.

after childbirth, which hormone stimulates the mammary glands to produce milk? oxytocin estrogen glucagon prolactin prolactin from the anterior pituitary stimulates milk production. oxytocin from the posterior pituitary causes milk ejection ("let-down") from the ducts, not production.

how do endocrine glands deliver their hormones to target cells? they release hormones through ducts onto the skin they empty hormones into the digestive tract they secrete hormones into the bloodstream they pass hormones directly along nerve axons endocrine glands are ductless; their hormones diffuse into nearby capillaries and travel in the blood. exocrine glands (sweat, salivary) use ducts to release secretions onto a surface or into a cavity.

which of the following are endocrine glands? select all that apply. thyroid gland adrenal glands pituitary gland salivary glands sweat glands the thyroid, adrenal glands, and pituitary secrete hormones directly into the blood. salivary and sweat glands are exocrine glands; they release their products through ducts.

steroid hormones such as cortisol and estrogen bind to receptors located inside target cells. why can they reach these receptors? they are pumped in by sodium–potassium pumps they are lipid-soluble and cross the plasma membrane they are large proteins that enter through channels they are carried into cells attached to red blood cells steroid hormones are made from cholesterol, so they are lipid-soluble. they pass through the phospholipid bilayer and bind receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus, often changing gene expression. water-soluble protein hormones such as insulin cannot cross the membra

a hormone travels in the blood to every part of the body, yet it affects only certain cells. why? only its target cells have receptors for that hormone the hormone is destroyed in all other tissues first only target cells are reached by the blood supply the hormone can only travel in one direction a cell can respond to a hormone only if it has the matching receptor. cells without the receptor are exposed to the hormone but do not respond.

which organ produces most of the testosterone in males? prostate gland adrenal medulla thymus testes interstitial (leydig) cells in the testes produce testosterone, under the control of lh from the anterior pituitary. the prostate makes part of the seminal fluid but does not produce testosterone.

tap the ball of capillaries where blood pressure pushes water and small solutes out of the blood to form filtrate. the glomerulus is a tuft of capillaries inside bowman's capsule. high pressure in the glomerulus forces water, ions, glucose and wastes like urea out of the blood. this is filtration. bowman's capsule is the cup around the glomerulus that collects the filtrate. it does not filter blood itself.

tap the part of the nephron that reabsorbs most of the filtrate: about two-thirds of the water and sodium and nearly all of the glucose. the proximal convoluted tubule (pct) comes right after bowman's capsule, in the cortex. its cells have microvilli, which give a large surface area for reabsorbing water, sodium, glucose and amino acids back into the blood. the loop of henle, dct and collecting duct fine-tune what is left.

put these structures in the order that filtrate flows through them, from first to last. bowman's capsule proximal convoluted tubule loop of henle distal convoluted tubule collecting duct filtrate forms in the glomerulus and is collected by bowman's capsule. it flows through the proximal convoluted tubule, then down and back up the loop of henle in the medulla. next is the distal convoluted tubule, which empties into a collecting duct shared by many nephrons. from there urine drains to the renal pelvis.

adh (antidiuretic hormone) inserts water channels into the tube that receives fluid from many nephrons, so more water is reabsorbed. tap that tube. the collecting duct receives fluid from the distal convoluted tubules of many nephrons and carries it through the medulla toward the renal pelvis. adh from the posterior pituitary makes the collecting duct more permeable to water, so the body keeps water and makes less, more concentrated urine. when a patient is dehydrated, adh goes up and urine becomes darker and more concentrated.

a patient with uncontrolled diabetes has glucose in the urine. normally, filtered glucose is reabsorbed almost completely. in which labeled structure does that reabsorption normally happen? a c e f glucose is filtered at the glomerulus (a) and normally reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule (c). the carriers in the pct can only move so much glucose. when blood glucose is very high, the filtered glucose overwhelms them and the extra spills into the urine. e is the loop of henle and f is the collecting duct. they do not reabsorb glucose.

tap the tube that carries urine from a kidney to the urinary bladder. each kidney has one ureter, a muscular tube that carries urine down to the bladder. the urethra is the single tube that carries urine from the bladder out of the body.

most urinary tract infections start when bacteria enter through the structure labeled e. what is structure e? ureter urinary bladder renal pelvis urethra e is the urethra, the tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body. bacteria from outside the body can travel up the urethra into the bladder (d). if not treated, the infection can climb the ureters (c) to the kidneys (b).

tap the structure where fertilization of an egg by a sperm usually occurs. after ovulation, the egg is swept into the uterine (fallopian) tube by its finger-like fimbriae. fertilization usually happens in the outer, wider part of the uterine tube. the early embryo then travels to the uterus to implant. the ovary releases the egg, but fertilization does not normally happen there.

an early embryo normally implants in layer d. what is layer d, and what happens to its outer part if pregnancy does not occur? myometrium; it contracts during labor endometrium; it is shed during menstruation cervix; it opens during ovulation endometrium; it stays thick until the next ovulation d is the endometrium, the inner lining of the uterus. it thickens each cycle to prepare for implantation. if no embryo implants, progesterone falls and the outer (functional) layer of the endometrium is shed as the menstrual flow. the myometrium (c) is the smooth muscle wall that contracts during labor.

put these organs in the order urine passes through them, from where it is formed to where it leaves the body. kidney ureter urinary bladder urethra urine forms in the kidneys and flows down the ureters to the urinary bladder, where it is stored. it leaves the body through the urethra.

put these parts of the nephron in the order that filtrate flows through them. glomerular (bowman's) capsule proximal convoluted tubule nephron loop (loop of henle) distal convoluted tubule collecting duct blood is filtered at the glomerulus, and filtrate enters the glomerular capsule. filtrate flows through the proximal convoluted tubule, the nephron loop, and the distal convoluted tubule. several nephrons drain into a collecting duct, where final water reabsorption is adjusted by adh.

what is the functional unit of the kidney, where urine is formed? neuron nephron alveolus renal pelvis each kidney has about a million nephrons, each of which filters blood and processes the filtrate into urine. the glomerulus is only the filtering part of the nephron; neurons and alveoli belong to other systems.

in which part of the nephron does filtration of blood plasma take place? glomerulus nephron loop (loop of henle) collecting duct distal convoluted tubule blood pressure pushes water and small solutes out of the glomerular capillaries into the glomerular capsule. blood cells and large proteins are normally too big to be filtered. the tubules and collecting duct handle reabsorption and secretion.

most reabsorption of water, glucose, amino acids, and sodium from the filtrate occurs in which part of the nephron? collecting duct glomerulus urinary bladder proximal convoluted tubule the proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs about two-thirds of the filtered water and sodium and normally all of the glucose and amino acids. its cells have microvilli that increase surface area for this work. the collecting duct fine-tunes water reabsorption, and the bladder only stores urine.

which of the following is normally not found in the urine of a healthy person? urea water red blood cells sodium ions blood cells are too large to pass through a healthy glomerular filter, so red blood cells in urine (hematuria) suggest disease, injury, or infection. urea, water, and sodium ions are normal components of urine.

a routine urinalysis shows glucose in a patient's urine. which condition is this most often associated with? severe dehydration from heat uncontrolled diabetes mellitus kidney stones blocking a ureter eating a high-protein diet normally, all filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. when blood glucose is very high, the filtrate contains more glucose than the transporters can reabsorb, so glucose spills into the urine (glycosuria). this is why untreated diabetes causes frequent urination and thirst.

a patient with chronic kidney disease often develops anemia. which hormone, normally made by the kidneys, is most likely deficient? erythropoietin renin insulin aldosterone the kidneys release erythropoietin (epo) when blood oxygen is low; epo stimulates red bone marrow to make red blood cells. damaged kidneys make less epo, so fewer red blood cells are made. renin is also made by the kidneys, but it regulates blood pressure, not red blood cell production.

urea, the main nitrogen-containing waste in urine, is produced from the breakdown of fatty acids glucose cholesterol amino acids when amino acids are broken down, their nitrogen-containing amino groups form toxic ammonia. the liver converts ammonia into less toxic urea, which the kidneys excrete. fats and carbohydrates contain no nitrogen, so they do not produce urea.

urinary tract infections are more common in females than in males. what is the main anatomical reason? females have only one kidney the female bladder is lined with skin the female urethra is much shorter females lack ureters the female urethra is only about 4 cm long and opens close to the anus, so bacteria can reach the bladder more easily. the male urethra is about 20 cm long, which makes it harder for bacteria to travel up it.

how do the kidneys help correct blood that has become too acidic? by excreting bicarbonate and reabsorbing h⁺ ions by excreting h⁺ ions and reabsorbing bicarbonate by releasing extra carbon dioxide gas into the urine by producing hydrochloric acid the kidneys secrete hydrogen ions into the urine and return bicarbonate (a base) to the blood. both actions raise blood ph back toward the normal range of about 7.35–7.45. the lungs, not the kidneys, adjust co₂.

drinking alcohol inhibits the release of antidiuretic hormone (adh). what is the expected effect on urine? a larger volume of more dilute urine a smaller volume of more concentrated urine glucose appears in the urine urine production stops completely adh normally tells the collecting ducts to reabsorb water. with less adh, less water is reabsorbed, so more water stays in the urine: more urine, and more dilute. this water loss is one reason alcohol contributes to dehydration.

in which structure does fertilization of an egg by a sperm normally occur? uterus ovary vagina uterine (fallopian) tube after ovulation, the egg is swept into the uterine tube, where it is usually fertilized. the resulting embryo travels to the uterus over several days and implants in the uterine lining.

in a healthy person, which substances are normally reabsorbed from the kidney filtrate back into the blood? select all that apply. water glucose amino acids creatinine excess hydrogen ions (h⁺) most filtered water and essentially all filtered glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed, mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule. creatinine, a muscle waste product, is not reabsorbed and is excreted in urine. excess h⁺ ions are secreted into the filtrate to help control blood ph, not reabsorbed.

put these structures in the order sperm pass through them, from production to exit. seminiferous tubules epididymis ductus (vas) deferens ejaculatory duct urethra sperm form in the seminiferous tubules and mature in the epididymis. during ejaculation they travel through the ductus deferens and ejaculatory duct into the urethra. a vasectomy cuts the ductus deferens, so sperm can no longer reach the urethra.

which event directly triggers ovulation, the release of an egg from the ovary? a sudden drop in estrogen levels a sharp rise in prolactin levels a surge of luteinizing hormone (lh) a surge of insulin from the pancreas as a follicle matures, rising estrogen triggers a sharp lh surge from the anterior pituitary. the lh surge causes the mature follicle to rupture and release the egg, about midway through the cycle. home ovulation tests detect this lh surge.

in a normal pregnancy, the embryo implants in which layer of the uterus? myometrium endometrium perimetrium cervix the endometrium is the inner, blood-rich lining that thickens each cycle to receive an embryo. the myometrium is the thick smooth-muscle layer that contracts during labor, and the perimetrium is the outer covering.

home pregnancy tests detect which hormone in urine? human chorionic gonadotropin (hcg) luteinizing hormone (lh) follicle-stimulating hormone (fsh) antidiuretic hormone (adh) soon after implantation, the developing placenta secretes hcg. hcg keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone, which maintains the uterine lining in early pregnancy.

if pregnancy does not occur, menstruation begins about two weeks after ovulation. what directly causes the uterine lining to shed? a surge of luteinizing hormone from the pituitary estrogen levels rise sharply in the bloodstream the ovary releases a second egg into the uterine tube progesterone falls as the corpus luteum breaks down after ovulation, the corpus luteum secretes progesterone (and estrogen), which maintains the thickened endometrium. without hcg from a pregnancy, the corpus luteum degenerates and progesterone drops. without progesterone support, the endometrium breaks down and is

which of the following are functions of the kidneys? select all that apply. filtering wastes from the blood helping regulate blood pressure by releasing renin producing erythropoietin storing urine until it is released producing bile the kidneys filter blood, help control blood pressure (renin), and release erythropoietin to stimulate red blood cell production. the urinary bladder stores urine, and the liver produces bile.

the tube that carries urine from the urinary bladder to the outside of the body is the ______. the urethra drains the bladder to the outside. do not confuse it with the ureter, which carries urine from a kidney to the bladder (there are two ureters but only one urethra).

an older man has trouble starting urination and a weak urine stream. enlargement of which gland, which surrounds the urethra just below the bladder, is the most likely cause? testes epididymis prostate gland thyroid gland the prostate wraps around the first part of the male urethra. when it enlarges with age (benign prostatic hyperplasia), it squeezes the urethra and obstructs urine flow.

tap the layer of skin that is made of stratified squamous epithelium and has no blood vessels of its own. the epidermis is the outer layer. it is stratified squamous epithelium with keratin on its surface. it has no blood vessels. its cells get nutrients by diffusion from capillaries in the dermis below. that is why a shallow scrape of only the epidermis does not bleed.

tap the gland that releases oily sebum into the hair follicle. sebaceous (oil) glands sit beside hair follicles in the dermis and empty sebum into the follicle. sebum keeps hair and skin soft and helps slow bacterial growth. a blocked follicle full of sebum can become acne. sweat glands release watery sweat through their own ducts and pores.

on a cold morning, "goosebumps" appear when a tiny smooth muscle pulls a hair upright. tap that muscle. the arrector pili muscle is a small band of smooth muscle that runs from the hair follicle to the upper dermis. cold or fear triggers sympathetic nerves that make it contract. the hair stands up and the skin around it puckers into a goosebump. it is smooth (involuntary) muscle, so you cannot make goosebumps on purpose.

layer e is made mainly of which type of tissue? stratified squamous epithelium dense irregular connective tissue adipose (fat) tissue skeletal muscle e is the hypodermis (subcutaneous layer), below the dermis. it is mostly adipose tissue with loose connective tissue. it insulates the body, cushions it and stores energy. stratified squamous epithelium is the epidermis (b). dense irregular connective tissue makes up most of the dermis (c).

during a central valley heat wave, which labeled structure cools the body by releasing a watery fluid onto the skin surface? d f g i d is a sweat gland. its coiled part sits deep in the dermis, and its duct opens at a pore on the skin surface. sweat cools the body as it evaporates. in extreme heat, a patient can lose a lot of water and salt this way. f (sebaceous gland) releases oil, not watery sweat. i (blood vessels) help cooling by widening, but they do not release fluid onto the skin.

which of the following structures in the diagram are located in the dermis? select all that apply. sebaceous gland arrector pili muscle hair shaft above the skin surface keratin-filled surface cells hair follicle the dermis is the thick connective-tissue layer under the epidermis. it holds hair follicles, sebaceous glands, arrector pili muscles, sweat glands, blood vessels and nerves. the hair shaft above the surface is outside the skin, and keratin-filled surface cells are the top of the epidermis.

a nurse gives a tuberculosis (tb) skin test as an intradermal injection, which raises a small bump just under the surface. type the name of the skin layer the medicine goes into. "intra-" means within, and "dermal" refers to the dermis. an intradermal injection places a small amount of fluid in the dermis. a subcutaneous injection goes deeper, into the hypodermis. an intramuscular injection goes into muscle below that.

what is the outermost layer of the skin? dermis hypodermis (subcutaneous layer) epidermis periosteum the epidermis is the thin, outer layer of stratified squamous epithelium. the dermis lies beneath it, and the hypodermis lies beneath the dermis. the periosteum covers bone.

a nurse gives an intramuscular injection in the upper arm. put these layers in the order the needle passes through them, from the surface inward. epidermis dermis hypodermis (subcutaneous layer) skeletal muscle the needle passes through the epidermis and then the dermis, which contains blood vessels and nerves. next is the fatty hypodermis (where subcutaneous injections such as insulin are given), and finally the deltoid muscle.

put the layers (strata) of the epidermis of thick skin, such as the palm, in order from the surface to the deepest layer. stratum corneum stratum lucidum stratum granulosum stratum spinosum stratum basale the deepest layer, the stratum basale, contains dividing stem cells. as cells are pushed upward through the spinosum and granulosum, they fill with keratin and die. thick skin has an extra clear layer, the lucidum, under the outermost layer of dead, flat cells, the stratum corneum.

compared with lightly pigmented skin, darkly pigmented skin typically has many more melanocytes spread through every layer of the epidermis similar numbers of melanocytes that make more melanin melanocytes located in the dermis instead of the epidermis a much thicker dermis that blocks ultraviolet light people of all skin tones have roughly similar numbers of melanocytes in the stratum basale. differences in skin color come mainly from how much and what type of melanin those melanocytes make and pass to keratinocytes.

which cells make up most of the epidermis and produce the tough protein that waterproofs and protects the skin? keratinocytes melanocytes fibroblasts adipocytes keratinocytes are about 90% of epidermal cells and produce keratin. melanocytes produce melanin, fibroblasts make collagen in the dermis, and adipocytes are fat cells in the hypodermis.

the skin begins the production of which vitamin when exposed to ultraviolet (uvb) light? vitamin c vitamin k vitamin b12 vitamin d uvb light converts a cholesterol derivative in the skin into a vitamin d precursor. the liver and kidneys then convert it into active vitamin d (calcitriol), which promotes calcium absorption.

which of the following structures are located in the dermis? select all that apply. blood vessels sweat glands hair follicles stratum corneum stratum basale the dermis is a connective tissue layer containing blood vessels, nerves, glands, and hair follicles. the stratum corneum and stratum basale are layers of the epidermis, which has no blood vessels; that is why a shallow scrape may not bleed.

insulin is usually injected into the hypodermis (subcutaneous layer). this layer is composed mainly of stratified squamous epithelium dense regular connective tissue like tendons adipose and loose connective tissue smooth muscle the hypodermis lies beneath the dermis and is mostly fat (adipose) with loose connective tissue. it insulates, cushions, stores energy, and anchors the skin to underlying muscle.

sebaceous glands secrete an oily substance into hair follicles. what is this substance called? sweat sebum keratin melanin sebaceous (oil) glands secrete sebum, which softens and waterproofs hair and skin and slows bacterial growth. when sebum and dead cells clog a follicle, acne can develop.

which glands release watery sweat over most of the body surface and are most important for cooling the body? eccrine sweat glands apocrine sweat glands sebaceous glands ceruminous glands eccrine glands are widespread and secrete watery sweat that cools the body as it evaporates. apocrine glands in the armpits and groin produce a thicker secretion that bacteria break down, causing body odor. ceruminous glands make earwax.

a patient has a burn that is red, very painful, and has blisters. the burn involves the epidermis and part of the dermis. how is it classified? first-degree (superficial) burn third-degree (full-thickness) burn fourth-degree burn second-degree (partial-thickness) burn first-degree burns involve only the epidermis: red and painful but no blisters (like a mild sunburn). blisters mean damage has reached into the dermis, which is a second-degree (partial-thickness) burn. third-degree burns destroy the epidermis and dermis completely.

a patient's third-degree burn appears leathery and white but is not painful when touched. what is the best explanation? the epidermis has already grown back over the burn melanocytes are blocking the pain signals nerve endings in the dermis have been destroyed swelling in the hypodermis is pressing on the muscles a full-thickness burn destroys the entire epidermis and dermis, including the sensory nerve endings. with no nerve endings, the burn itself may feel numb, while the partial-thickness burns around it are painful. these burns usually need skin grafts because the regenerating cells are g

an adult is burned over the entire left arm and the entire front of the trunk. using the rule of nines (each arm = 9%, front of trunk = 18%), what percentage of the total body surface area is burned? add the regions: left arm 9% + anterior trunk 18%. 9 + 18 = 27% of the total body surface area. estimating burn size this way helps the team calculate fluid replacement.

when the body gets cold, how do blood vessels in the dermis respond? they dilate, bringing more warm blood to the skin surface they constrict, reducing heat loss through the skin they fill with sweat to insulate the body they move into the epidermis vasoconstriction sends less warm blood to the skin surface, so less heat is lost to the air. in heat, the opposite happens: dermal vessels dilate and the skin flushes, releasing heat.

"goosebumps" form when tiny muscles attached to hair follicles contract. what are these muscles called? arrector pili muscles erector spinae muscles intercostal muscles myoepithelial cells arrector pili are small smooth muscles that pull hairs upright when you are cold or frightened. this produces goosebumps; in furry animals it traps a warmer layer of air.

a patient's lips and nail beds look bluish. this sign, called cyanosis, most likely indicates liver disease excess melanin production a vitamin d deficiency low blood oxygen hemoglobin that is low in oxygen is darker, so poorly oxygenated blood gives skin a bluish tint. yellow skin (jaundice) points to liver problems, and melanin produces brown tones.

where are new cells produced that make a fingernail grow longer? the free edge the nail plate's tip the nail matrix the cuticle (eponychium) the nail matrix at the base of the nail, under the skin, is where cells divide. the new keratinized cells push the nail plate forward toward the free edge. the cuticle is a fold of skin that covers the base of the nail; it does not produce the nail.

which type of skin cancer is most dangerous because it is most likely to spread (metastasize) to other organs? basal cell carcinoma melanoma squamous cell carcinoma seborrheic keratosis melanoma arises from melanocytes and spreads readily, so it is the deadliest skin cancer. basal cell carcinoma is the most common but rarely spreads; squamous cell carcinoma spreads occasionally; seborrheic keratosis is a benign growth. check moles with abcde: asymmetry, border, color, diameter, evolving.

which of the following are functions of the integumentary system? select all that apply. protecting against pathogens and water loss helping regulate body temperature beginning vitamin d synthesis producing red blood cells storing bile skin is a barrier to microbes and dehydration, regulates temperature through sweat and blood flow, and begins vitamin d synthesis. red blood cells are made in red bone marrow, and bile is stored in the gallbladder.

the brown pigment produced by melanocytes that absorbs ultraviolet radiation is called ______. melanocytes in the stratum basale make melanin and pass it to keratinocytes. melanin forms a protective cap over each cell's nucleus, shielding dna from uv damage.

in which layer of the epidermis do stem cells divide by mitosis to produce new keratinocytes? stratum basale stratum corneum stratum granulosum stratum lucidum the stratum basale (basal layer) sits on the basement membrane next to the dermis, where it can get nutrients by diffusion. its cells divide continuously, pushing older cells up toward the surface, where they die and flake off from the stratum corneum.

a patient who has been bedridden for weeks develops a pressure injury (bedsore) over the sacrum. what is the main cause? too much melanin in the skin overactive sebaceous glands clogging the pores excess vitamin d production in the skin constant pressure cuts off blood flow to the tissue constant pressure over a bony area squeezes the capillaries in the skin. without blood flow, cells do not get oxygen and nutrients and begin to die. turning patients regularly relieves pressure and helps prevent these injuries.

tap the organelle that makes most of the cell's atp through cellular respiration. mitochondria carry out the oxygen-using steps of cellular respiration, which produce most of a cell's atp. in the drawing, the mitochondria are the bean-shaped organelles with folded inner membranes (cristae). the folds add surface area for making atp. the nucleus stores dna and the golgi packages proteins. neither one is the cell's main atp producer.

structure k is a stack of membranes studded with ribosomes. what is its main job? breaking down worn-out organelles and cell debris making lipids and helping the liver detoxify drugs making proteins that will be secreted or placed in membranes storing the cell's dna and controlling gene expression k is the rough endoplasmic reticulum (rough er). the dots on it are ribosomes, so it builds proteins. proteins made on the rough er are sent to the golgi apparatus and are then secreted, put into membranes, or delivered to lysosomes. making lipids and detoxifying drugs is the job of the smooth er (h)

this diagram shows an animal cell. which of the labeled structures would a typical plant cell also have? select all that apply. nucleus mitochondrion centrioles cell membrane golgi apparatus plant and animal cells are both eukaryotic, so both have a nucleus, mitochondria, a cell membrane, er, ribosomes and a golgi apparatus. most plant cells do not have centrioles. they still build a spindle for mitosis, but without centrioles. plant cells also have structures that animal cells lack: a cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole.

the panels show the same kind of cell at five points in the cell cycle, but they are out of order. put the panels in order from first to last. panel b panel e panel d panel a panel c b is interphase: the nuclear envelope is intact and the dna is loose chromatin. e is prophase: the chromosomes condense into x shapes and the nuclear envelope breaks down (dashed). d is metaphase: the chromosomes line up at the middle. a is anaphase: the sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles. c is telophase: two new nuclei form and the cell begins to pinch in two (cytokinesis).

tap the cell in which sister chromatids have separated and are moving toward opposite poles. in anaphase the centromeres split and spindle fibers pull the sister chromatids apart, so each pole gets one complete set of chromosomes. in the drawing, the chromatids form v shapes with the centromere leading toward each pole. in metaphase the chromosomes are still doubled (x-shaped) and lined up at the middle. in telophase the chromosomes are already inside two new nuclei.

which organelle produces most of a cell's atp through cellular respiration? mitochondrion ribosome golgi apparatus lysosome mitochondria carry out the aerobic steps of cellular respiration, which make most of the cell's atp. ribosomes build proteins, the golgi packages and ships proteins, and lysosomes digest wastes.

proteins are polymers built from which monomers? amino acids nucleotides monosaccharides fatty acids and glycerol amino acids are joined by peptide bonds to make polypeptides (proteins). nucleotides build nucleic acids, monosaccharides build carbohydrates, and fatty acids plus glycerol build triglycerides (fats).

which structure is found in plant cells but not in animal cells? cell membrane mitochondria ribosomes cell wall plant cells have a rigid cellulose cell wall outside the cell membrane; animal cells do not. both plant and animal cells have a cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes.

cells of the pancreas make and secrete large amounts of digestive enzymes, which are proteins. which organelle would you expect to be especially abundant in these cells? rough endoplasmic reticulum smooth endoplasmic reticulum lysosomes centrioles rough er is studded with ribosomes and makes proteins that will be secreted from the cell. smooth er makes lipids and detoxifies; lysosomes digest materials; centrioles help organize cell division.

which statement correctly describes prokaryotic cells such as bacteria? they lack a membrane-bound nucleus. they lack ribosomes. they lack dna. they lack a cell membrane. "prokaryote" means "before nucleus": the dna sits in a nucleoid region with no membrane around it. prokaryotes still have dna, ribosomes and a cell membrane—all living cells do.

during which phase of mitosis do sister chromatids separate and move to opposite ends of the cell? prophase metaphase telophase anaphase in anaphase the centromeres split and the spindle pulls sister chromatids toward opposite poles. chromosomes condense in prophase, line up in the middle in metaphase, and new nuclei form in telophase.

what is the result of mitosis followed by cytokinesis in a human body cell? four haploid daughter cells that are genetically different two haploid daughter cells that are genetically identical four diploid daughter cells that are genetically different two diploid daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent mitosis makes copies for growth and repair, so the two daughter cells keep the full (diploid) chromosome set and identical dna. four genetically different haploid cells is the result of meiosis.

crossing over, the exchange of dna between homologous chromosomes, occurs during which stage? prophase i of meiosis prophase of mitosis anaphase ii of meiosis telophase i of meiosis homologous chromosomes pair up only in meiosis i; while paired in prophase i they swap segments. mitosis never pairs homologous chromosomes, so crossing over does not happen there.

a human cell entering meiosis has 46 chromosomes. right after meiosis i is complete, what does each daughter cell contain? 23 chromosomes, each made of a single chromatid 23 chromosomes, each made of two sister chromatids 46 chromosomes, each made of two sister chromatids 46 chromosomes, each made of a single chromatid meiosis i separates homologous pairs, so the chromosome number drops from 46 to 23. the sister chromatids have not separated yet—that happens in meiosis ii—so each of the 23 chromosomes is still doubled.

which type of molecule forms the basic double-layer structure of cell membranes? glycogen phospholipids nucleic acids cellulose phospholipids have water-loving (hydrophilic) heads and water-fearing (hydrophobic) tails, so they arrange into a bilayer. glycogen is stored carbohydrate, nucleic acids store genetic information, and cellulose forms plant cell walls.

which statement about enzymes is correct? they are used up in the reactions they speed up. they speed up reactions by raising the activation energy. they speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy. most of them are carbohydrates. enzymes are biological catalysts: they lower the energy barrier so a reaction happens faster. catalysts are not consumed, and most enzymes are proteins, not carbohydrates.

a red blood cell is placed in a hypertonic salt solution. what happens to the cell? water enters the cell, and the cell swells and bursts. nothing happens because the solution is the same as the cell's interior. salt leaves the cell, and the cell swells. water leaves the cell, and the cell shrinks. hypertonic means the solution outside has more solute (less water) than the cell. by osmosis, water moves out of the cell toward the higher solute concentration, so the cell shrinks (crenates). swelling and bursting happens in a hypotonic solution; no change happens in an isotonic one such as 0.9% s

what is the main function of ribosomes? building proteins storing genetic information breaking down worn-out organelles controlling what enters the cell ribosomes read mrna and link amino acids together to make proteins. the nucleus stores dna, lysosomes break down old parts, and the cell membrane controls what enters.

starch, glycogen and cellulose are all polymers made from which monomer? amino acids glucose fructose glycerol all three are polysaccharides made of many glucose units; they differ in how the glucose units are linked and branched. amino acids build proteins and glycerol is part of fats; fructose is a sugar but is not the building block of these three.

which process requires the cell to spend atp? o₂ diffusing from blood into a muscle cell water entering a cell through aquaporins a na⁺/k⁺ pump moving na⁺ against its gradient glucose moving down its gradient via a carrier moving a substance against its concentration gradient (low to high) is active transport and requires energy, usually atp. diffusion, osmosis and facilitated diffusion all move substances down their gradients and are passive—no atp needed.

which structures are found in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells? select all that apply. ribosomes cell membrane dna nucleus mitochondria every cell has a cell membrane, ribosomes to make proteins, and dna. only eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria.

which statements correctly describe meiosis? select all that apply. it produces gametes (eggs and sperm). it includes two rounds of cell division. its daughter cells are genetically identical to the parent cell. it reduces the chromosome number by half. it is how skin cells divide to heal a cut. meiosis has two divisions (meiosis i and ii) and makes haploid gametes with half the chromosome number. crossing over and independent assortment make the daughter cells genetically different. skin cells heal wounds by mitosis, not meiosis.

put these stages of the cell cycle in order, starting with interphase. interphase (dna is copied) prophase metaphase anaphase telophase dna replicates during interphase, before mitosis begins. then: prophase (chromosomes condense), metaphase (line up in the middle), anaphase (chromatids pull apart), telophase (two nuclei form).

a typical human body cell has 46 chromosomes. how many chromosomes are in a normal human egg cell? eggs and sperm are made by meiosis, which halves the chromosome number. 46 ÷ 2 = 23, so fertilization (23 + 23) restores 46.

a human cell has 46 chromosomes before dna replication. after the s phase of interphase, how many chromatids does the cell contain? during the s phase each chromosome is copied, so each one is now made of two sister chromatids. the chromosome count is still 46, but the chromatid count is 46 × 2 = 92.

in this dna segment, which base belongs in the box marked "?" thymine (t) adenine (a) guanine (g) uracil (u) the base across from the "?" is thymine (t). in dna, adenine always pairs with thymine (a–t) and guanine always pairs with cytosine (g–c). so the missing base is adenine. uracil is found in rna, not dna. t does not pair with another t.

once the "?" base is filled in correctly, how many hydrogen bonds in total hold the two strands of this 5-base-pair segment together? each a–t pair is held by 2 hydrogen bonds, and each g–c pair is held by 3. the dashed lines in the drawing show this. the pairs from top to bottom are a–t, g–c, c–g, t–a, and g–c. 2 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 13 hydrogen bonds.

tap the structure where translation (protein synthesis) takes place. translation happens at a ribosome in the cytoplasm. the ribosome reads the mrna three bases (one codon) at a time. in the drawing, the ribosome is made of two subunits that clamp onto the mrna. a chain of amino acids comes out of the top. transcription, which makes mrna from dna, happens in the nucleus. that is not translation.

one codon on the dna template strand in this gene reads 3′-tac-5′. which mrna codon is made from it during transcription? 5′-atg-3′ 5′-uac-3′ 5′-aug-3′ 5′-tac-3′ during transcription, rna bases pair with the dna template: a→u, t→a, c→g, g→c. t pairs with a, a pairs with u, and c pairs with g, so tac is copied into aug. "atg" is wrong because rna uses uracil (u) instead of thymine (t). "uac" and "tac" just repeat or swap the template bases instead of pairing them.

put these steps in making a protein in order, from first to last. part of the dna unwinds, and an mrna copy of a gene is made in the nucleus the mrna leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore a ribosome attaches to the mrna in the cytoplasm trna molecules bring amino acids that match each mrna codon the amino acids are linked into a growing polypeptide chain transcription comes first. in the nucleus, dna is used as a template to build mrna. the mrna exits through a nuclear pore, and a ribosome attaches to it in the cytoplasm. during translation, trnas carry in amino acids that match the codons
in a dna molecule, adenine (a) pairs with which base? uracil (u) guanine (g) cytosine (c) thymine (t) in dna, a pairs with t and g pairs with c. uracil replaces thymine only in rna.

which nitrogen base is found in rna but not in dna? uracil thymine adenine cytosine rna uses uracil in place of thymine. adenine, guanine and cytosine are found in both dna and rna; thymine is only in dna.

what happens during transcription? a protein is built from an mrna template at a ribosome. an mrna molecule is made from a dna template. a dna molecule is copied to make a second dna molecule. trna molecules link amino acids into a chain. transcription copies the information in a gene into messenger rna; in eukaryotes this happens in the nucleus. building a protein at the ribosome is translation, and copying dna is replication.

a section of a dna template strand reads tacgga. what is the complementary mrna sequence? atgcct uacgga augccu auggcu pair each dna base with its rna partner: t→a, a→u, c→g, g→c. t a c g g a → a u g c c u. atgcct uses t, which rna doesn't have; uacgga just copies the strand instead of pairing it.

a stretch of mrna contains 36 nucleotides. every nucleotide is read as part of a codon, and none of the codons is a stop codon. how many amino acids does it code for? each codon is 3 nucleotides and codes for 1 amino acid. 36 ÷ 3 = 12 amino acids.

which molecule carries amino acids to the ribosome and has an anticodon that pairs with a codon on mrna? messenger rna (mrna) ribosomal rna (rrna) dna polymerase transfer rna (trna) trna has an anticodon on one end and the matching amino acid on the other. mrna carries the codons, rrna forms part of the ribosome, and dna polymerase copies dna.

in pea plants, tall (t) is dominant over short (t). two tt plants are crossed. what fraction of the offspring are expected to be tall? 3/4 1/4 1/2 4/4 (all) punnett square: tt, tt, tt, tt. three of four boxes have at least one t, so 3/4 are tall. 1/4 is the fraction that is short (tt).

in a certain plant, purple flowers (p) are dominant over white flowers (p). a pp plant is crossed with a pp plant. what percent of the offspring are expected to have white flowers? 0% 50% 25% 75% punnett square for pp × pp: pp, pp, pp, pp. two of four boxes are pp (white), so 2/4 = 50%.

brown eyes (b) are dominant over blue eyes (b) in this simplified example. two parents are both bb. what percent of their children are expected to be bb? punnett square for bb × bb: bb, bb, bb, bb. one of four boxes is bb: 1/4 = 25%.

two pea plants that are both heterozygous for two traits (aabb × aabb) are crossed. both traits show complete dominance and the genes assort independently. what phenotype ratio is expected in the offspring? 3 : 1 1 : 2 : 1 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 a dihybrid cross of two double heterozygotes gives a 16-box punnett square. 9 dominant–dominant : 3 dominant–recessive : 3 recessive–dominant : 1 recessive–recessive. 3 : 1 is a monohybrid ratio; 1 : 2 : 1 is a monohybrid genotype ratio; 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 comes from aabb × aabb.

a plant with genotype aabb is crossed with an aabb plant. the genes assort independently. what fraction of the offspring are expected to be aabb? 1/16 3/16 1/2 1/4 treat each gene separately: aa × aa gives aa 1/2 of the time; bb × bb gives bb 1/2 of the time. multiply: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. 1/16 is the aabb fraction for aabb × aabb, not this cross.

a trait is controlled by a dominant allele h and a recessive allele h. a person has genotype hh. which description is correct? heterozygous, showing the dominant phenotype homozygous dominant, showing the dominant phenotype heterozygous, showing the recessive phenotype homozygous recessive, showing the recessive phenotype two different alleles (h and h) means heterozygous. with complete dominance, one h is enough to show the dominant trait.

a red-flowered snapdragon is crossed with a white-flowered snapdragon, and all the offspring have pink flowers. what pattern of inheritance does this show? codominance incomplete dominance sex-linked inheritance complete dominance the heterozygote shows a blend (pink) between the two parent phenotypes, which is incomplete dominance. in codominance both traits show fully at once (for example, ab blood type), not a blend.

red–green color blindness is an x-linked recessive trait. a color-blind man (xᶜy) and a woman who has two normal alleles (xx) have children. which statement is correct? all sons will be color-blind; daughters will be unaffected. half of the daughters will be color-blind. all daughters will be carriers; no sons will be color-blind. half of the sons will be carriers of the allele. the father passes his xᶜ to every daughter and his y to every son. daughters get xᶜ from dad and a normal x from mom: carriers (xᶜx), not color-blind. sons get their only x from mom, which is normal, so they are unaffe

deleting one nucleotide near the beginning of a gene usually has a large effect on the protein. why? it changes only one amino acid in the protein. it removes an entire chromosome from the cell. it converts the gene from dna into rna. it shifts the reading frame, changing every codon after the deletion. mrna is read three bases at a time; removing one base shifts how every later codon is grouped. this frameshift usually changes many amino acids or creates an early stop codon. a single-base substitution, not a deletion, is what typically changes just one amino acid.
what sugar is found in dna nucleotides? deoxyribose ribose glucose sucrose dna = deoxyribonucleic acid, named for its sugar, deoxyribose. ribose is the sugar in rna.

which statements correctly describe differences between dna and rna? select all that apply. dna is usually double-stranded, while rna is usually single-stranded. rna contains uracil instead of thymine. rna contains the sugar ribose, while dna contains deoxyribose. dna is built from amino acids, while rna is built from nucleotides. only rna has a phosphate group in its backbone. dna: double helix, deoxyribose, thymine. rna: usually single strand, ribose, uracil. both are built from nucleotides, and both have sugar–phosphate backbones.

put these steps of protein synthesis in order from first to last. a gene in the dna is transcribed into mrna in the nucleus. the mrna moves out of the nucleus to a ribosome. trna anticodons pair with the mrna codons at the ribosome. amino acids are joined by peptide bonds to form a polypeptide. dna → mrna (transcription) happens first, in the nucleus. the mrna travels to a ribosome, where trnas read it codon by codon (translation) and their amino acids are linked into a chain.

use the codon table to answer. codon meaning aug methionine (start) uuu phenylalanine ggc glycine uaa stop an mrna reads aug uuu ggc uaa. how many amino acids does this mrna code for? 2 3 4 12 aug = methionine, uuu = phenylalanine, ggc = glycine: 3 amino acids. uaa is a stop codon. it ends translation and does not add an amino acid, so 4 is a trap. 12 is the number of nucleotides, not amino acids.

dna replication is described as semiconservative. what does this mean? both strands of each new dna molecule are newly made. each new dna molecule has one original strand and one newly made strand. the original dna molecule stays intact, and the copy is entirely new. each strand is a random mix of old and new pieces. the double helix unzips and each original strand serves as a template for a new partner strand. so each daughter molecule "conserves" half of the original: one old strand plus one new strand.

tap the structure the bacterium uses to swim through fluid. a flagellum is a long, whip-like tail. it spins like a propeller to move the bacterium. the short hair-like pili on the top surface help bacteria stick to surfaces, such as the lining of the urinary tract. they are not used for swimming.

penicillin kills bacteria by stopping them from building one of the labeled layers. which letter shows that layer? a c d j penicillin blocks the building of peptidoglycan, the main material of the bacterial cell wall (c). without a strong wall, the bacterium swells and bursts. a is the capsule and d is the cell membrane, which lies inside the wall. j is the envelope of the virus, and viruses have no cell wall at all.

which of the following are found in the bacterium but not in the virus? select all that apply. ribosomes cytoplasm genetic material plasmid protein capsid a bacterium is a living cell. it has cytoplasm, ribosomes to make its own proteins, and often small rings of extra dna called plasmids. a virus is not a cell. it has genetic material (dna or rna) inside a protein capsid, and some viruses also have a lipid envelope. it must use a host cell's ribosomes. both have genetic material, so that choice is wrong. only the virus has a capsid.

tap the protein shell that directly encloses the virus's genetic material. the capsid is the protein coat (shown as a hexagon) that surrounds the virus's rna or dna. in an enveloped virus, the capsid is in turn wrapped in a lipid envelope that carries spike proteins. the envelope comes from the host cell's membrane. the spikes and the envelope are on the outside. the capsid is the layer touching the genetic material.

a patient with a sore throat caused by a virus like the one shown asks for antibiotics. which statement best explains why antibiotics will not help? the virus's envelope is too thick for antibiotics to get through viruses are larger than bacteria, so the usual dose is too small the virus's spike proteins break down antibiotics on contact the virus has no cell wall or ribosomes of its own for antibiotics to attack antibiotics work by attacking structures and processes that bacteria have, such as the cell wall or bacterial ribosomes. a virus has none of these. it is genetic material inside a pro

which of the following is not made of cells? a bacterium a yeast a virus an amoeba viruses are acellular: genetic material inside a protein coat, with no cytoplasm, ribosomes or metabolism of their own. bacteria are prokaryotic cells; yeasts (fungi) and amoebas (protozoa) are eukaryotic cells.

a patient with a cold asks for antibiotics. why won't antibiotics help? cold viruses are too large for antibiotics to reach them. the immune system blocks antibiotics during a cold. colds are caused by fungi, which resist all drugs. colds are viral, and viruses lack what antibiotics target. antibiotics attack bacterial features such as cell walls and bacterial ribosomes. viruses have no cell wall or ribosomes of their own, so antibiotics have nothing to act on. viruses are also much smaller than bacteria.

how does penicillin kill bacteria? it blocks the building of the bacterial cell wall. it destroys the protein coat of viruses. it dissolves the bacterial nuclear membrane. it makes the patient produce more antibodies. penicillin interferes with peptidoglycan cell-wall synthesis, so the bacterium bursts as it grows. human cells have no cell wall, which is why penicillin can target bacteria. bacteria have no nuclear membrane at all.

why do gram-positive bacteria stay purple after a gram stain? their thin peptidoglycan layer is covered by an outer membrane. their thick peptidoglycan cell wall traps the crystal violet dye. they have a nucleus that absorbs the purple dye. they have no cell wall, so the dye soaks in. a thick peptidoglycan layer holds the crystal violet–iodine complex even when alcohol is applied. a thin wall with an outer membrane describes gram-negative bacteria, which lose the purple and pick up the pink counterstain.

after a gram stain is completed, what color do gram-negative bacteria appear under the microscope? purple green pink to red colorless alcohol washes the crystal violet out of gram-negative cells, leaving them colorless for a moment. the last step adds safranin, which stains them pink to red.

valley fever, common in california's central valley, is caught by breathing in spores of coccidioides from dust and soil. what type of pathogen causes valley fever? bacterium virus protozoan fungus coccidioides is a fungus that lives in dry soil; disturbing the soil (farming, construction, wind) releases its spores. because it is a fungus, it is treated with antifungal drugs, not antibiotics.

which pairing of a disease with the type of organism that causes it is correct? malaria — protozoan influenza — bacterium tuberculosis — virus athlete's foot — protozoan malaria is caused by plasmodium , a protozoan spread by mosquitoes. influenza is viral, tuberculosis is bacterial, and athlete's foot is fungal.

spherical bacteria that grow in grape-like clusters are called streptococci staphylococci bacilli spirilla "coccus" means sphere and "staphylo-" means grape-like cluster. streptococci are spheres in chains, bacilli are rods, and spirilla are spirals.

over many years, a bacterial population becomes resistant to an antibiotic. which explanation is best? bacteria choose to change their dna after exposure to the drug. the patient's body becomes resistant and stops absorbing the drug. bacteria with random resistance mutations survive and multiply. the antibiotic itself mutates into a weaker form in the body. resistance comes from natural selection: mutations arise randomly, the antibiotic kills susceptible cells, and the survivors multiply. bacteria don't "decide" to mutate, and it's the bacteria—not the patient or the drug—that become resistan

which describes the basic structure of a virus? cytoplasm and ribosomes surrounded by a cell wall a nucleus surrounded by a cell membrane chloroplasts surrounded by a protein coat genetic material (dna or rna) inside a protein coat a virus is nucleic acid wrapped in a protein capsid; some also have an outer envelope. ribosomes, cytoplasm, nuclei and chloroplasts are features of cells.

how do viruses reproduce? they use a host cell's machinery to make new viruses. they split in two by binary fission, like bacteria. they form spores that grow on their own in soil. they divide by mitosis, like human body cells. viruses have no metabolism of their own, so they can only replicate inside a host cell. binary fission is how bacteria reproduce; mitosis is how eukaryotic cells divide.

bacteria usually reproduce by which process? meiosis binary fission mitosis fertilization a bacterium copies its circular chromosome and splits into two identical cells: binary fission. mitosis and meiosis involve a nucleus, which bacteria don't have.

which of these microorganisms is a eukaryote? escherichia coli streptococcus saccharomyces (baker's yeast) influenza virus yeasts are fungi, and fungi are eukaryotes with a nucleus. e. coli and streptococcus are bacteria (prokaryotes); a virus is not a cell at all.

antifungal drugs tend to cause more side effects in humans than many antibacterial drugs do. what is the best explanation? fungi are prokaryotes, so they are harder to reach. fungi have no cell membrane, so drugs must be stronger. antifungal drugs are made from weakened viruses. fungal cells are eukaryotic, much like human cells. a good drug hits something the microbe has and we don't. bacteria (prokaryotes) differ from us in many ways: cell walls, ribosomes and more. fungal cells share most of their structures with human cells, so drugs that harm fungi are more likely to harm our cells too.

clinics sterilize instruments in an autoclave with pressurized steam at about 121 °c instead of just boiling them. boiling water may not destroy which of the following? bacterial endospores viral envelopes protozoan cilia fungal hyphae some bacteria (such as clostridium and bacillus ) form endospores—tough, dormant structures that survive boiling at 100 °c. pressurized steam reaches a higher temperature and kills endospores. viral envelopes, cilia and hyphae are easily destroyed by heat.

which of these diseases are caused by bacteria? select all that apply. strep throat tuberculosis influenza valley fever most urinary tract infections strep throat ( streptococcus ), tuberculosis ( mycobacterium ) and most utis (often e. coli ) are bacterial. influenza is caused by a virus, and valley fever is caused by a fungus.

which features do bacteria have that viruses do not have? select all that apply. ribosomes a cell membrane can be targeted by antibiotics genetic material a need to always be inside a host cell to reproduce bacteria are cells: they have ribosomes and a cell membrane, which antibiotics can target. both bacteria and viruses carry genetic material. always needing a host cell to reproduce describes viruses, not bacteria in general.

a bacterial population doubles every 20 minutes. if a wound culture starts with 100 bacteria, how many bacteria will there be after 2 hours, assuming nothing limits growth? 2 hours = 120 minutes; 120 ÷ 20 = 6 doublings. 100 → 200 → 400 → 800 → 1,600 → 3,200 → 6,400. or 100 × 2⁶ = 100 × 64 = 6,400.

put the steps of the gram stain in order from first to last. add crystal violet (primary stain) add iodine (mordant) rinse with alcohol (decolorizer) add safranin (counterstain) crystal violet stains all cells purple; iodine locks it in. alcohol removes the purple from gram-negative cells only; safranin then stains those cells pink.

after a sierra backpacking trip, a hiker who drank untreated stream water develops diarrhea. the cause is giardia , a single-celled organism with a nucleus that swims using flagella. giardia is best classified as a bacterium protozoan virus fungus single-celled, eukaryotic (has a nucleus), and moves on its own: that describes a protozoan. bacteria lack a nucleus, viruses are not cells, and fungi don't swim with flagella like this.

this bohr model shows a neutral atom. which element is it? sodium (atomic number 11) magnesium (atomic number 12) vanadium (atomic number 23) neon (atomic number 10) an element is identified by its number of protons (its atomic number). the nucleus shows 11 protons, so this is sodium. magnesium is the trap for students who count the 12 neutrons. vanadium is the trap for adding protons and neutrons together (11 + 12 = 23, which is the mass number). neon has 10 electrons in total. this atom has 2 + 8 + 1 = 11 electrons, which matches its 11 protons.

tap the shell that holds this atom's valence electron. valence electrons are the electrons in an atom's outermost occupied shell. this atom has electrons arranged 2, 8, 1, so its single valence electron is in the third (outer) shell. the inner shells hold core electrons, which do not usually take part in bonding.

when this atom reacts with chlorine, what is it most likely to do? gain 7 electrons and become a 7− ion lose 1 proton and become a 1− ion lose 1 electron and become a 1+ ion share 7 electrons and form a covalent bond the atom (sodium) has 1 valence electron. losing that one electron leaves a full outer shell of 8 electrons, which is much easier than gaining 7. after losing 1 electron, it has 11 protons and 10 electrons, so its charge is 1+ (na⁺). it then forms an ionic bond with cl⁻. protons never change during a chemical reaction. changing the number of protons would turn the atom into a diff

tap the element in period 3 that has the same number of valence electrons as oxygen. elements in the same group (column) have the same number of valence electrons. oxygen is in group 16, so it has 6 valence electrons. period 3 is the third row. the group 16 element in that row is sulfur (s), which also has 6 valence electrons. phosphorus (group 15) has 5 valence electrons, and chlorine (group 17) has 7.

tap the element in this table with the highest electronegativity. electronegativity is how strongly an atom pulls on shared electrons in a bond. it increases from left to right across a period and from bottom to top in a group. that puts the most electronegative element at the top right. fluorine (f) is the most electronegative of all elements. the noble gases (he, ne, ar) are usually left out because they rarely form bonds.

which lettered element is most likely to form an ion with a 2+ charge? a b c e group 2 elements (the alkaline earth metals) have 2 valence electrons and lose both to form 2+ ions. a is magnesium (mg) in group 2, so it forms mg²⁺. e is potassium (group 1), which forms k⁺. c is chlorine, which gains an electron to form cl⁻. b is silicon, a metalloid that usually shares electrons instead of forming ions.

which subatomic particle has a negative charge? proton neutron electron nucleus electrons are negative, protons are positive, and neutrons have no charge. the nucleus is not a particle; it is the center of the atom that holds protons and neutrons.

the atomic number of an element tells you the number of neutrons in the nucleus protons plus neutrons valence electrons protons in the nucleus atomic number = number of protons, and it defines the element (every carbon atom has 6 protons). protons plus neutrons is the mass number.
chlorine-37 has an atomic number of 17. how many neutrons are in one atom of chlorine-37? neutrons = mass number − atomic number. 37 − 17 = 20 neutrons.

isotopes of the same element have different numbers of neutrons protons electrons in the neutral atom atomic numbers isotopes have the same number of protons (same element) but different numbers of neutrons, so their mass numbers differ. changing the protons would change the atomic number and make a different element.

which statement about carbon-12 and carbon-14 is correct? carbon-14 has 2 more protons than carbon-12. both have 6 protons; carbon-14 has 2 more neutrons. neutral carbon-14 has 2 more electrons than neutral carbon-12. they are different elements because they have different masses. both are carbon, so both have 6 protons (and 6 electrons when neutral). carbon-12 has 12 − 6 = 6 neutrons; carbon-14 has 14 − 6 = 8 neutrons: 2 more.

magnesium has atomic number 12. how many electrons does a mg²⁺ ion have? 2 10 12 14 a neutral mg atom has 12 electrons. the 2+ charge means it lost 2 electrons: 12 − 2 = 10. 14 would be adding electrons, which would make a negative ion.
sulfur has atomic number 16. how many electrons are in a sulfide ion, s²⁻? neutral sulfur has 16 electrons. a 2− charge means 2 extra electrons: 16 + 2 = 18.

how many valence electrons does an oxygen atom have? (oxygen is in group 16.) 2 6 8 16 for main-group elements in groups 13–18, valence electrons = group number − 10. oxygen: 16 − 10 = 6. electron configuration check: 1s² 2s² 2p⁴ → 2 + 4 = 6 in the outer shell. 8 is a full octet, which oxygen reaches by gaining 2 electrons (o²⁻).

which of these elements has the highest electronegativity? oxygen nitrogen fluorine carbon electronegativity increases from left to right across a period and from bottom to top in a group. fluorine is at the top right (excluding noble gases), making it the most electronegative element.

sodium, magnesium, aluminum and chlorine are all in period 3. which has the largest atomic radius? magnesium aluminum chlorine sodium across a period, protons are added while the shell number stays the same, so the stronger nuclear pull shrinks the atoms. sodium, at the far left, is the largest; chlorine is the smallest of these.

which of these atoms has the largest atomic radius? potassium (k) lithium (li) sodium (na) fluorine (f) atomic radius increases going down a group because each row adds an electron shell. li, na and k are all in group 1; k is lowest, so it is largest. f is in period 2 at the right side, so it is very small.

why are noble gases such as neon and argon very unreactive? they have no electrons. their outer (valence) electron shells are full. their nuclei have no protons. they are always solids at room temperature. noble gases already have a stable, full valence shell (8 electrons, or 2 for helium), so they rarely gain, lose or share electrons. they do have protons and electrons, and they are gases at room temperature.

metals such as sodium and calcium tend to gain electrons and form negative ions share electrons and form only covalent bonds lose electrons and form positive ions gain protons and form positive ions metals have few valence electrons and low electronegativity, so they give electrons away and become cations. ions form by gaining or losing electrons, never protons—changing protons would change the element.

why do elements in the same group (column) of the periodic table have similar chemical properties? they have the same atomic mass. they have the same number of neutrons. they have the same number of electron shells. they have the same number of valence electrons. chemical behavior depends mostly on valence electrons, and elements in a group share the same valence count (for example, all group 1 metals have 1). elements in the same period, not group, have the same number of occupied shells.

an element has two isotopes: one with mass 10 amu (20% abundance) and one with mass 11 amu (80% abundance). what is the average atomic mass? 10.2 amu 10.5 amu 10.8 amu 11.0 amu weighted average: (10 × 0.20) + (11 × 0.80). 2.0 + 8.8 = 10.8 amu. 10.5 is a simple average that ignores abundance; the answer must be closer to 11 because that isotope is more common.

a neutral atom of sodium-23 has atomic number 11. which statements about it are correct? select all that apply. it has 11 protons. it has 12 neutrons. it has 23 electrons. it has 1 valence electron. its mass number is 11. protons = atomic number = 11, and a neutral atom has the same number of electrons (11, not 23). neutrons = 23 − 11 = 12. mass number is 23. sodium is in group 1, so it has 1 valence electron.

which of these elements are halogens (group 17)? select all that apply. fluorine chlorine sodium argon iodine group 17, the halogens: fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine. sodium is an alkali metal (group 1) and argon is a noble gas (group 18).

elements in the same period (row) of the periodic table have the same number of occupied electron shells number of valence electrons atomic mass chemical reactivity the period number tells how many electron shells (energy levels) are occupied: period 3 elements use three shells. same valence electrons is the pattern for groups (columns), not periods.

which pair shows the ions that calcium (group 2) and chlorine (group 17) usually form? ca²⁻ and cl⁺ ca²⁺ and cl⁻ ca⁺ and cl²⁻ ca²⁺ and cl⁷⁺ calcium has 2 valence electrons and loses both: ca²⁺. chlorine has 7 valence electrons and gains 1 to complete its octet: cl⁻. together they form cacl₂.

an atom has 15 protons, 16 neutrons and 15 electrons. what is its mass number? 15 16 30 31 mass number = protons + neutrons = 15 + 16 = 31. electrons are not counted; 30 is the trap of adding protons and electrons.

tap the box that shows the reactants. reactants are the substances you start with. they are on the left side of the arrow in an equation, which is the "before" box here. the "after" box shows the product, ammonia (nh₃), which forms when nitrogen (n₂) and hydrogen (h₂) react.

use the particle diagram to balance the equation: __n₂ + __h₂ → __nh₃ using the lowest whole numbers, what coefficient goes in front of h₂? count the molecules. the before box has 2 n₂ and 6 h₂, and the after box has 4 nh₃. that ratio is 2 : 6 : 4. divide each number by 2 to get the lowest whole numbers: 1 : 3 : 2. the balanced equation is n₂ + 3h₂ → 2nh₃. check: n is 2 on the left and 2 × 1 = 2 on the right. h is 3 × 2 = 6 on the left and 2 × 3 = 6 on the right.

which statements are supported by the particle diagram? select all that apply. the number of nitrogen atoms is the same before and after the reaction the number of hydrogen atoms is the same before and after the reaction the number of molecules is the same before and after the reaction this is a synthesis (combination) reaction some mass is destroyed during the reaction atoms before: n = 2 × 2 = 4 and h = 6 × 2 = 12. atoms after: n = 4 × 1 = 4 and h = 4 × 3 = 12. the atoms are the same, so mass is conserved. the number of molecules changes from 8 (2 n₂ + 6 h₂) to 4 (nh₃). atoms are conserved,

what type of bond holds the nitrogen and hydrogen atoms together within the molecule labeled c? ionic bond, because electrons are transferred covalent bond, because electrons are shared hydrogen bond, because the molecule contains hydrogen metallic bond, because nitrogen is a metal c is ammonia (nh₃). nitrogen and hydrogen are both nonmetals, and nonmetals bond to each other by sharing electrons. that is a covalent bond (here, a polar covalent bond). ionic bonds form between a metal and a nonmetal, such as na⁺ and cl⁻. a hydrogen bond is a weaker attraction between molecules, not the bond that

which type of reaction does the particle diagram show? decomposition single replacement synthesis combustion two reactants (n₂ and h₂) combine to form one product (nh₃). that pattern, a + b → ab, is a synthesis (combination) reaction. decomposition is the reverse (ab → a + b). single replacement swaps one element for another. combustion needs o₂ and usually makes co₂ and h₂o.

which compound is held together by ionic bonds? co₂ h₂o nacl ch₄ ionic bonds form between a metal and a nonmetal when electrons are transferred: na⁺ and cl⁻. co₂, h₂o and ch₄ contain only nonmetals, so they are covalent.

in a covalent bond, atoms transfer electrons from one atom to another share protons form ions with opposite charges share pairs of electrons covalent bonds form when two atoms (usually nonmetals) share one or more pairs of electrons. transferring electrons makes ions and ionic bonds.

the o–h bonds in a water molecule are polar covalent bonds. why? oxygen is more electronegative, so the shared electrons are pulled closer to oxygen. hydrogen is more electronegative, so the electrons are pulled toward hydrogen. oxygen completely transfers its electrons to hydrogen. oxygen and hydrogen share the electrons exactly equally. oxygen pulls on shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen does. this unequal sharing gives oxygen a partial negative charge (δ−) and each hydrogen a partial positive charge (δ+). equal sharing would be nonpolar; full transfer would be ionic.

hydrogen bonds between water molecules are best described as covalent bonds between two h atoms in the same molecule attractions between δ+ h on one molecule and δ− o on another ionic bonds between h⁺ ions and oh⁻ ions in the water shared electron pairs between o atoms of neighboring molecules a hydrogen bond is an attraction between molecules, not a true bond within a molecule. it forms when h bonded to o, n or f is attracted to a lone pair on an o, n or f of a neighboring molecule. hydrogen bonds explain water's high boiling point and surface tension.

in the dna double helix, what holds the two strands together? ionic bonds between sugars peptide bonds between amino acids hydrogen bonds between paired bases covalent bonds between phosphate groups on opposite strands a–t and g–c base pairs are held together by hydrogen bonds (2 for a–t, 3 for g–c). these relatively weak attractions let the strands unzip for replication and transcription. peptide bonds are found in proteins.

what type of reaction is 2h₂ + o₂ → 2h₂o? decomposition single replacement double replacement synthesis (combination) two reactants combine into one product: a + b → ab is synthesis. (this reaction is also a combustion of hydrogen.)
what type of reaction is caco₃ → cao + co₂? decomposition synthesis single replacement combustion one reactant breaks into two simpler products: ab → a + b is decomposition.

what type of reaction is zn + 2hcl → zncl₂ + h₂? double replacement single replacement decomposition synthesis one element (zn) replaces another (h) in a compound: a + bc → ac + b. double replacement swaps partners between two compounds.
